documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern business environments, fundamentally reshaping how organizations collect information, generate knowledge, make decisions, and create value. The convergence of AI and Business Intelligence (BI) enables enterprises to move beyond descriptive reporting toward predictive and prescriptive decision-making frameworks. Simultaneously, entrepreneurs and startups increasingly employ AI-powered analytics, intelligent automation, and machine learning to identify market opportunities, optimize operations, and develop innovative products and services. This article examines the evolving relationship between AI, Business Intelligence, and entrepreneurship, highlighting how organizations leverage data-driven intelligence for sustainable competitive advantage and organizational innovation. Drawing upon contemporary research and practical examples, the article explores technological foundations, leadership implications, entrepreneurial opportunities, global and local applications, and future challenges. The discussion emphasizes that successful adoption of AI requires not only technical capabilities but also strategic leadership, ethical governance, and a culture of continuous innovation.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Within the hospitality industry, the continuing introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is attracting increasing attention. Although there is a rapidly growing literature on the role of AI within the industry, how specific companies have publicly reported on their introduction of AI has attracted little or no attention in the business and management literature. This gap highlights a broader challenge regarding the absence of a structured approach to AI deployment, leaving stakeholders with limited visibility of how organizations are managing the associated risks. Using an interpretivist inductive approach, this exploratory paper first looks to contribute to helping to fill that gap by providing a narrative synthesis of relevant literature and some case examples of how four major hotel groups, namely Hilton Worldwide Holdings, Marriott International, International Hotel Group (IHG) Hotels and Resorts, and Wyndham Hotels and Resorts are introducing AI. The main process “touchpoints” where AI is impacting hospitality operators are identified and the key challenges and potential downsides of AI deployment are outlined. To cope with these challenges, drawing on the case examples and the literature, the paper then puts forward a structured Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) based framework rooted in the ISO/IEC 42001 AI Management System standard. This approach offers a practical and auditable pathway for mitigating risks such as data privacy violations, algorithmic bias, and operational disruptions. This will be of relevance not only to researchers but also to hotel operators looking to progress AI change projects responsibly and strategically within their operations.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid digitalization of tourism has increased the demand for intelligent recommendation systems capable of delivering personalized travel experiences that adapt to users' evolving preferences and contextual circumstances.Conventional tourism recommendation platforms predominantly rely on static filtering mechanisms and explicit user ratings, often producing generic recommendations that fail to reflect dynamic travel behaviors and real-time contextual information.This study presents the design, development, and evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based travel recommendation system that integrates explicit user preferences, implicit behavioral analytics, contextual awareness, sentiment analysis, and machine learning techniques to enhance personalized tourism experiences in Nigeria.Adopting a mixed-methods research design within a Design Science Research (DSR) framework, the study combines quantitative surveys, behavioral data acquisition, system development, and experimental evaluation.Tourist demographic information, browsing history, clickstream behavior, geo-location data, travel reviews, and contextual variables were collected and preprocessed through data cleaning, normalization, feature engineering, and sentiment extraction before model training.The proposed hybrid recommendation engine combines collaborative filtering, content-based recommendation, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and contextual recommendation algorithms to generate adaptive travel suggestions based on continuously evolving user interactions.Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the hybrid model outperforms conventional recommendation approaches, achieving superior recommendation accuracy, ranking quality, user engagement, and satisfaction.The incorporation of explainable AI mechanisms and ethical data governance further enhances transparency, user trust, and responsible AI

This article argues for a new class of digital legal subject within AI legal-personhood doctrine — the ‘AI-digital human’ — largely unaddressed in domestic and international legal scholarship. Building on the author’s earlier three-class model of AI legal subjects and the institution of the AI-representative, the article distinguishes two different modules of the AI-digital human: Module 1 (Digiperson), a digital human as a functional reflection of a specific natural person, built on ‘red-group’ identification attributes and digitised access credentials; and Module 2 (autonomous Digihuman), reflecting no real natural person, its attributes formed referentially and tied to a functional role within a digital ecosystem. The article shows that equating a digital human with a natural person in the full scope of rights and obligations is a doctrinal error: legal status should follow an age-based logic (child—adolescent—adult) rather than mirroring the prototype’s status. Drawing on a comparative analysis of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) and Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2.0), the article substantiates the need for a Digital Humans Registry as an institutional legitimation mechanism for both modules, and formulates draft articles for the Ukrainian Law on Artificial Intelligence.

This research examines how artificial intelligence and machine learning can automate and improve data governance across cloud data platforms. It focuses on intelligent metadata management, automated data lineage tracking, and continuous regulatory compliance monitoring. The proposed framework integrates machine learning for metadata inference and data classification, graph-based techniques for lineage tracking, and automated compliance rules for detecting potential violations. It also explores natural language processing, data discovery, impact analysis, explainable AI, and human-in-the-loop review. The paper discusses implementation strategies, integration challenges, model accuracy, data drift, and the importance of human oversight for sensitive governance decisions. It provides practical guidance for organizations seeking to scale data governance while improving visibility, consistency, and compliance across cloud and hybrid environments. Keywords: AI-Driven Governance, Data Lineage, Metadata Management, Compliance Automation, Cloud Data Platforms, Machine Learning.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an important driver of transformation in supply chain management (SCM). Existing research has focused primarily on consumer-facing contexts and localized applications such as forecasting, inventory, and logistics. Comparatively less attention has been given to how leading manufacturing firms implement AI to support SCM processes in real-world production contexts. To address this gap, this study adopts a case study approach to examine Foxconn’s BOMate platform as an example of AI-enabled supply chain management in advanced electronics manufacturing. The current case in study focuses on the AI-driven platform design principles which integrate experts’ rules, big data and AI modeling to augment procurement decision-making. The findings illustrate that BOMate contributes to SCM in several important ways. First, it augments human decision-making by combining expert rules, accumulated sourcing knowledge, and AI-based processing within a human-AI collaborative framework. Second, it enhances sourcing efficiency by accelerating component retrieval, substitute identification, and decision support. More broadly, the case suggests that AI in Foxconn’s supply chain is not limited to localized automation, but supports system-level coordination across procurement, production, and supply chain operations. This study contributes to the literature by providing empirical insight into AI-enabled SCM in a leading manufacturing firm and highlights the strategic importance of AI in improving supply chain efficiency, resilience, and technological transformation.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of everyday work. Workers use it to prepare documents and evaluate information, while some may encounter it through systems that assign or assess their work. Research has examined productivity, organizational adoption, collaboration, and algorithmic management. These studies offer important evidence but tell us less about how workers experience AI as part of their daily work. In this conceptual paper, I apply occupational science to AI-mediated work. I argue that patterned and situated AI-related activity can be examined as occupation: it takes shape within workplace routines, can carry meaning for workers, and can affect their opportunities to participate. Drawing on occupational science and selected AI-at-work scholarship, I propose an analytic map with seven elements: human–AI actions, work integration, interpretive work, responsibility work, relational work, identity work, and boundary work. I consider how workplace conditions shape these elements and their consequences for workers. This perspective connects questions about AI at work with workers’ experience of what they do and what their contribution means.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support product management tasks. At the same time, AI-native research and development (R&D) may increase software realization capacity. Organizations may realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be realized. This paper asks how product management should be re-envisioned under these conditions. We synthesize research on software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the Product Management and R&D boundary. We propose a vision in which AI becomes a persistent participant in product work. The vision covers sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. We propose six principles and make the vision tangible through an operating model grounded in human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context. We further argue that AI-native Product Management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Finally, we identify four AI-specific research directions that require empirical investigation.

Recruitment is an important function of Human Resource Management, but traditional recruitment processes become difficult to manage when organizations receive a large number of job applications.Manual resume screening, subjective interview evaluation and limited use of recruitment data can increase the time required for hiring and may introduce inconsistency and bias into candidate selection.This paper presents an AI Recruitment and Talent Analytics System that combines Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine learning(ML),Natural Language Processing(NLP), and data analytics to support an intelligent recruitment workflow.The proposed system automates major stages of recruitment, beginning with candidate registration and resume submission.NLP-based resume processing is used to extract skills, education, certifications, and work experience.Candidate profiles are compared with job requirements to support candidate-job matching and ranking.The system also proposes an AI-based interview module for evaluating technical knowledge, communication abilities, behavioral responses, and overall performance.A recruitment analytics dashboard provides candidate rankings, hiring insights, reports, and decision-support information.The current prototype focuses on the landing page, authentication interface, candidate dashboard, HR dashboard, and AI interview interface, providing a foundation for subsequent backend, database, AI/ML, and predictive analytics integration.

Strategic management settled its dispute between environmental determinism and managerial choice by treating constraint as arriving from outside the firm. Artificial intelligence unsettles that arrangement, because the algorithms that filter markets, rank acquisition targets and evaluate strategic alternatives are installed by executives themselves. This conceptual paper asks where executive agency goes when strategic decisions pass through algorithmic systems. Drawing on upper echelons and managerial discretion research, sociomaterial accounts of technology and evidence on how decision-makers respond to algorithmic outputs, it develops a framework of configured discretion. Algorithmic determinism is theorized as an endogenous, cumulative constraint operating through attention, evaluation and capability. Executive agency is relocated into three practices: framing objectives, contesting outputs and reconfiguring decision architecture. The central argument is that delegation is self-binding. Each act of delegation can erode the capabilities executives need to contest the system later, so formal authority persists while real latitude shrinks. Seven propositions follow, with a state-transition model of four adaptation states (algorithmic capture, governed hybridity, executive voluntarism and fragmented drift) that recasts the two-continua model of organizational adaptation for firms whose constraints are partly self-made. The framework reconciles conflicting findings on algorithm aversion and appreciation and on the value of human override. Governance regimes moderate the loop: fiduciary duties of care and oversight, audit-committee benchmarks against core models and party-state oversight each shape how far effective discretion can fall below formal authority.

documents.abstract: Algorithmic learning of algebraic structures connects computability theory with artificial intelligence. Classical inductive inference mainly deals with formal languages and recursive functions. In contrast, analyzing vector spaces allows us to explore the theoretical limits of automated scientific discovery. This study investigates the algorithmic learnability of subspace families in computable vector spaces over a computable field. We focus on the fundamental family of all finite-dimensional subspaces and examine whether learnability is an isomorphism invariant. By combining constructive model theory with Gold’s paradigm of identification in the limit, our results identify the exact recursion-theoretic barriers to learning algebraic invariants. We use the classical model of explanatory learning in the limit from positive data (Ex-learning), where Turing machines act as learners. By applying canonical index numberings of finite sets and effective quotient space constructions, we establish two fundamental theorems. Our first result shows that if a computable vector space has a decidable linear dependence relation, the family of all its finite dimensional subspaces is Ex-learnable.. Second, we construct a computable vector space where the relation of linear dependence is undecidable. By using an effective priority-style diagonalization argument, we prove that the family of finite-dimensional subspaces in this space fails to be Ex learnable. These results prove that algorithmic learnability is not an isomorphism invariant of an abstract algebraic structure. Instead, it is strictly governed by the algorithmic complexity (Turing degree) of the linear dependence predicate. This finding provides a theoretical foundation for automated theorem proving and neuro-symbolic AI systems.

Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

Health issues are among the major concerns for people nowadays. Cancer remains one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, and many are suffering from it. Out of these, skin cancer is also one of its kind and the deadliest. According to estimates, the number of new melanoma cases has surged in recent years, and the death rate from these instances has also sharply increased. By 2040, the number of melanoma cases will have sharply increased if this trend continues. So, finding and diagnosing it in the earliest stage is one of the most powerful and best ways to improve a skin cancer patient’s chance of survival. It is also essential to determine the type of cancer to ensure effective treatment. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has shown remarkable progress in medical image analysis, especially in Machine Learning and Deep Learning, for detecting and classifying skin cancer types. There are many revolutionary changes with the CNN models. Even though CNNs have become popular, these networks are called black boxes because we are unsure where the models focus in input images.These results are insufficient for medical practitioners to confirm it.Therefore, we require additional information on the model's explainability. Visual Interpretability is one of the techniques we used to address this issue. Grad-CAM is one of the XAI tools for visualizing where a CNN Network focuses. In this work, we focus on seven types of skin cancer. We trained the proposed IMSCNN+Grad-CAM model, along with state-of-the-art image classification models.The proposed model, IMSCNN+Grad-CAM, outperforms well, achieving an accuracy of 96.87%. Wealso compared and cross-verified the results of CNN models with Grad-CAM-generated images to ensure them. From this, we analysed our results and found that our proposed IMSCNN+Grad-CAM Model is a more suitable approach for skin cancer image classification and explainability problems.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the way businesses understand consumers, analyse behavioural patterns, and make marketing and business decisions. The present study, “An Empirical Study on AI-Driven Consumer Insights,” examines the role of AI in generating consumer insights, analysing consumer behaviour, influencing purchasing decisions, improving personalised marketing, and supporting business decision-making. The study also considers the importance of ethical AI practices, privacy, transparency, trust, and responsible use of consumer data. Primary data were collected from 128 respondents from Mumbai, and the data were analysed using tabulation and the Chi-Square test. The findings indicate statistically significant responses across all six hypotheses. The results suggest that respondents perceive AI as an important tool for generating consumer insights, improving consumer behaviour analysis, influencing purchasing decisions, enhancing personalised marketing, and supporting business decisions. The findings also highlight the importance of ethical AI practices in consumer data collection. The study concludes that AI-driven consumer insights can provide significant value to businesses when implemented effectively, transparently, and responsibly. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Consumer Insights, Consumer Behaviour, Personalised Marketing, Purchasing Behaviour, Business Decision-Making, Ethical AI.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The recent rapid advancement in artificial intelligence technologies has brought about a fundamental transformation in higher education and scientific research institutions by providing new opportunities to enhance interdisciplinary learning and cognitive integration across various scientific fields. This study aimed to propose an integrative model based on artificial intelligence to analyze the impact of using AI tools in enhancing interdisciplinary learning and scientific research among postgraduate students at the Libyan Academy–Janzour. The study adopted the descriptive-analytical approach, and data were collected from a sample of (94) master's and doctoral students using a questionnaire specifically designed for this purpose. The reliability test results indicated that the study instrument possessed a high degree of reliability, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of (0.912). The results of the descriptive analysis indicated that the sample members possessed a high level of digital competence, with a mean score of (3.92) and a standard deviation of (0.64). The findings also revealed a high impact of using artificial intelligence tools on improving the quality of scientific research and research productivity, with a mean score of (4.15) and a standard deviation of (0.58), in addition to a positive role in enhancing interdisciplinary integration, with a mean score of (3.88) and a standard deviation of (0.71). Furthermore, the results of the inferential analysis showed no statistically significant differences in the participants' attitudes toward the proposed model attributed to academic specialization (F = 1.42, p = 0.241) or academic level (t = 0.85, p = 0.398), which confirms the applicability of the model across various specializations and academic levels. Additionally, the findings revealed a strong, statistically significant positive correlation between digital competence and interdisciplinary research integration (r = 0.684, p < 0.001), indicating that developing digital skills directly contributes to enhancing students' ability to employ artificial intelligence tools in producing more integrated and interdisciplinary research. The study findings confirm that artificial intelligence represents an effective tool for supporting interdisciplinary integration, improving scientific research efficiency, and facilitating knowledge exchange and academic collaboration across different disciplines. This study also contributes to enriching the scientific literature related to the employment of artificial intelligence in higher education and provides a practical framework that can be utilized in developing smart academic environments that support interdisciplinary learning and scientific research.

Situation awareness (SA) is crucial for effective teaming and is becoming increasingly relevant in human-AI teaming as AI systems take on more active roles. AI systems rely on designed interactions to communicate information and coordinate with humans, which may influence how human teammates perceive, interpret, and anticipate task situations. Therefore, this scoping review synthesizes how SA is framed and examined in human-AI teaming from an interaction perspective, providing a coherent understanding of fragmented evidence across application domains. The review followed the JBI framework and was reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. We searched five databases on January 13, 2026: Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and PsycINFO. Studies were eligible if they involved humans and AI jointly engaging in a shared task, addressed SA or related constructs, and described interaction processes involving situational information exchange. Screening and data charting were independently conducted by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. We included 52 studies published between 2005 and 2025, mapping application domains, SA framing, teaming configurations, situational information used by AI systems, and reported interaction processes involving situational information exchange. The results showed that within the retrieved corpus, studies published in later years more frequently addressed non-domain-specific and everyday-life contexts. Interaction processes varied in information exchange direction, trigger, and functional role, with recurring patterns centered on AI-to-human information provision, modification of plans, and alignment of shared understanding. The synthesized interaction-centered framework offers a structured basis for future research on SA-oriented interaction design in human-AI teaming.

Rapid growth in IoT devices has led to the creation of crucial cybersecurity threats since existing methods of malware detection which use signature matching and numerical feature analysis are incapable of capturing the contextual behavioral semantics of IoT attacks. The presented work proposes an innovative malware detection framework incorporating a pipeline of behavior-to-text transformation together with transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform binary classification of IoT network traffic. Selected through the process of SHAP-based feature importance analysis, the numerical features of network flows from the initial set of 41 features are transformed into natural language descriptions, allowing encoder-based LLMs to capture the context of IoT traffic behavior. Four LLMs, including DistilBERT, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa, were fine-tuned and rigorously tested against four Deep Learning baselines, Neural Network, LSTM, BiLSTM, and CNN, and four Machine Learning baselines, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, using the CIC-IoT-2023 dataset under three experimental setups: balanced classification, realistic imbalanced distribution, and unseen variant detection. Additionally, a four-class multi-class classification experiment and an ablation study were conducted to further validate the framework. On a balanced dataset consisting of 400,000 samples, BERT-base and RoBERTa achieved the highest F1-scores of 98.94% with precision above 99.96%. In the imbalanced case of 90% attack and 10% benign traffic, the precision of all models was equal to 99.99%. The framework attained an F1-score of 99.99% for unseen variant detection on a completely unseen Mirai botnet variant with zero false negatives. The four-class multi-class experiment achieved a Macro F1-score of 88.80%. Statistical analysis across three independent runs confirmed high result stability with standard deviations below 0.03%. SHAP analysis revealed that packet count, ACK flag number, and HTTPS indicator were the most discriminative features, while attention visualization confirmed token-level interpretability. All LLMs consistently outperformed all Deep Learning baselines, providing evidence for the effectiveness of the behavior-to-text transformation paradigm for IoT malware detection, while classical ML models achieved marginally higher F1-scores due to their efficiency with numerical features, providing evidence for the effectiveness of the behavior-to-text transformation paradigm for IoT malware detection.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: This anatomical review examines Valerio Capraro's (2026) conceptualisation of LLMorphism—the biased belief that human cognition operates analogously to large language models (LLMs)—as introduced in arXiv:2605.05419. The paper is dissected sectionally: from its diagnosis of reverse inference arising from conversational fluency, through mechanisms of analogical transfer and metaphorical availability, to distinctions from adjacent constructs and projected societal impacts. Pros include the construct's novelty, careful differentiation, and timely intervention in public AI discourse; cons encompass its speculative character, absence of empirical validation, and under-specification of architectural dissimilarities between transformers and biological neural systems. At least ten competing models of mind and cognition—including predictive processing, embodied cognition, computationalism, enactivism, extended mind, dual-process theory, intentional stance, combinatorial creativity frameworks, argumentative theories of reasoning, and phenomenological accounts—are compared and contrasted. Ontological verticals (nature of cognition as embodied, agentic, and historically situated versus statistical pattern completion) and epistemological verticals (fluency as surrogate for justification; confabulation versus grounded inquiry) are analysed in depth. Possible extensions include psychometric operationalisation, cross-cultural validation, and integration with AI governance frameworks for digital sovereignty in the Global South. The review concludes that LLMorphism usefully names a cultural risk but requires empirical grounding to avoid itself becoming a reductive metaphor. KSCCN review article, 10 October 2026. Artificial intelligence increasingly supports human decision making, but effective use depends on whether users assign AI advice the decision weight it warrants. This theory-oriented narrative review synthesizes 29 core studies, together with recent reviews and foundational theory, to examine appropriate reliance, overreliance, and underreliance in AI-supported decisions. The synthesis identifies five recurring sociotechnical conditions shaping reliance: system, user, task, interaction, and organization. Findings show that explanations, uncertainty cues, expertise, self-confidence, prior experience, and organizational incentives affect reliance differently across settings, while trust and reliance evolve through feedback over time. Interventions that reduce overreliance may also increase underreliance. The resulting framework centers warranted behavioral decision weight, comparative evaluation of AI and self-capability, and temporal feedback, shifting attention from increasing trust or AI use toward supporting context-sensitive allocation of decision weight.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering every stage of medical education, yet guidance for responsible integration remains limited. We synthesize evidence across undergraduate, graduate, and continuing medical education within institutional, learning, and readiness and safety systems. Integration should reflect task structure, verifiability, consequence, and oversight. Continuing medical education remains comparatively underdeveloped despite its importance for practicing physicians, who use clinical AI directly and shape trainee practices, institutional adoption, and responsible implementation.

documents.abstract: Background Increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical workflows necessitates assessing how future healthcare professionals adapt to these technologies. Objectıve This study aims to determine the artificial intelligence literacy and anxiety levels of students at a Vocational School of Health Services (VSHS) and to analyze the factors influencing these levels. Methods This cross-sectional and descriptive-predictive study invited 800 associate degree healthcare students, resulting in a final sample of 545 participants (response rate: 68.12%). Instruments included a Sociodemographic Form, the AI Literacy Scale (AILS), and the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS). Results The mean age of participants was 20.41 ± 4.07 years. While 55.6 % of students reported partial knowledge of AI, only 44.4 % reported active use of AI-supported tools. documents.abstract: The growing accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies presents new opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve efficiency, customer engagement, decision-making and competitiveness. However, the level of AI adoption among SMEs remains uneven, particularly in developing economies where financial, technological and infrastructural constraints may limit effective utilization. This study examined the extent of AI adoption, its relationship with organizational performance, and the major constraints affecting adoption among SMEs in Anambra State, Nigeria, with particular focus on the Onitsha and Nnewi business clusters. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was employed. From a population of 1,200 registered SMEs, a sample of 300 owner-managers and managers was determined using Taro Yamane's formula and selected through proportionate stratified sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression with SPSS version 27 at the 5% level of significance. The findings revealed a moderate overall level of AI adoption, with relatively higher use of AI-supported customer communication and generative AI applications for marketing and content creation, while advanced applications for sales analysis, inventory management and personalization recorded lower usage. The regression results showed that AI adoption was positively associated with organizational performance (B = 0.576, β = .518, R² = .268, p < .001), indicating that higher levels of AI adoption corresponded with improved organizational performance. The major constraints to AI adoption were high implementation cost, inadequate AI and digital literacy, unreliable electricity supply, lack of technical expertise and poor or expensive internet connectivity. The study concludes that although AI adoption among SMEs in Anambra State remains moderate and uneven, its effective integration into business activities is associated with improved organizational performance. It therefore recommends practical AI-literacy programmes, affordable digital-financing support and improved electricity and internet infrastructure to facilitate wider and more effective adoption among SMEs.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into clinical gastroenterology, with emerging applications in nursing contexts. However, the extent and nature of these applications in gastroenterology nursing remain under-explored. This scoping review aimed to map the current landscape of AI and closely related AI-adjacent digital technologies in gastroenterology nursing. Methods: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guideline, PubMed, Medline, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for peer-reviewed, English-language studies published since 2000, and the findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 184 records identified, 11 studies were included, highlighting the potential of these technologies in clinical decision support, workflow optimization, patient education, and endoscopy assistance. Reported benefits include gains in workflow efficiency, technical accuracy, and reduced administrative workload; direct evidence of improved nursing-led patient outcomes was reported in only a minority of studies. Challenges encompass limited nurse-led research, insufficient external validation, implementation gaps, and ethical concerns. Conclusions: Greater nurse involvement in AI development is essential to drive paradigm shifts in clinical practice. This review synthesizes evidence to inform future applications, research, and policy in AI-enhanced gastroenterology nursing.

documents.abstract: Abstract* Background Artificial intelligence (AI), integrated with imaging technologies, is increasingly applied across orthodontic assessment and care pathways. However, the evidence remains scattered across imaging modalities, clinical applications, AI methodologies, and stages of clinical translation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2016 and June 2026, with searches supplemented by Google Scholar, OpenAlex, grey literature sources, and citation searching. Eligible studies were mapped descriptively and synthesised thematically using Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Fifty-four studies were included. AI applications used intraoral and facial photographs, cephalometric radiographs, CBCT, intraoral scans, three-dimensional dental models, and multimodal imaging. Applications ranged from landmark localisation, segmentation, and malocclusion classification to treatment-need assessment, screening, referral support, treatment planning, and remote monitoring. Evidence was strongest for bounded, anatomically verifiable image-analysis tasks, whereas applications involving referral, triage, treatment-need decisions, longitudinal prediction, and workflow integration were less mature. Common limitations included retrospective, single-centre designs; heterogeneous reference standards; limited external validation; inconsistent reporting of calibration and uncertainty; and insufficient evaluation of patient-centred, equity, and service-level outcomes. Conclusions Imaging-based AI in orthodontics has evolved from automated image interpretation to clinician-assisted decision support across the care pathway. Current evidence most strongly supports AI for structured image-analysis tasks, but does not yet support autonomous referral, triage, or treatment-planning decisions. Future research should prioritise prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, explainability, fairness, uncertainty handling, and workflow-integrated evaluation to enable safe and clinically useful implementation.

documents.abstract: The incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in judicial processes is perhaps the greatest technological innovation which has impacted legal systems globally. In India, there has been an increasing trend among the judicial systems towards adopting new technologies in order to increase efficiency, transparency, accessibility, and administration of justice. With the incorporation of technologies like e-Courts, virtual court sessions, electronic case management systems, and AI-enabled legal research tools, the groundwork has been laid for a technology-driven mechanism for administering justice. However, AI has not been adopted to replace judicial decision-making process in India but has been used to assist judges, lawyers, researchers, and court staff in performing monotonous and data-intensive tasks. These trends have become even more pertinent considering the huge number of pending cases and increasing need for justice.The present work will discuss how the use of AI has evolved in the Indian judicial system by considering the technological advancements made so far, judicial reforms, legal issues arising therefrom and possible future scenarios. The study will explore the benefits and risks associated with the use of AI in improving judicial efficiency in India. This study will adopt a doctrinal approach to qualitative research through constitutional provisions, court judgments, policies, government reports, and scholarly work. It contends that AI should only be viewed as assistive technology and not as something that should replace human judges.

Insurance claim analytics is often constrained by limited access to real-world data, which restricts the evaluation of advanced artificial intelligence approaches in practical insurance settings. Leveraging the SynthETIC framework, this study systematically evaluates classical actuarial models, neural-network-based methods, generative adversarial networks, and reinforcement learning for three core components of insurance claim processes: claim severity, incremental payments, and settlement delays. GAN-based data augmentation is implemented using task-specific architectures, including a tabular GAN for claim severity, an LSTM-based sequence GAN for incremental payments, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty for settlement delays, while Proximal Policy Optimization provides a sequential decision-learning framework for claim processes. Experimental results show that the performance of data-driven approaches is task-dependent, with GAN-based data augmentation improving some predictive measures but not consistently across all tasks and evaluation metrics. PPO-based reinforcement learning is more sensitive to task formulation and model design, reflecting the importance of action-space specification and reward structures. Additional experiments and mathematical analysis further examine the role of task-specific constraints in sequential payment allocation and delay prediction, highlighting the importance of admissible actions, state representation, and reward design. Overall, the findings illustrate how synthetic insurance environments can support the systematic evaluation of emerging AI paradigms and provide methodological insights into the task-dependent roles of GAN-based data augmentation and reinforcement learning in insurance claim analytics.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the emerging trends and applications of computing in libraries. It involves programming computers to do things, which if done by humans, would be said to require intelligence. The ultimate promise of artificial intelligence in libraries is to develop computer systems or machines that think, behave, and in fact rival human intelligence, and this clearly has major implications on librarian ship. The application of artificial intelligence in the library has become pervasive. They include expert systems for reference services, book reading and shelf-reading robots, virtual reality for immersive learning among others. Although the incorporation of artificial intelligence in libraries can be perceived to alienate librarians from their users, it will probably help libraries do more rather than taking over the jobs of librarians. It will enhance their services delivery. Artificial intelligence will greatly improve library operations and services and will upgrade and heighten the relevance of libraries in an ever-changing digital society.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in healthcare, from image-based diagnosis to patient-facing management tools, yet the supporting literature is fragmented across communities that rarely read one another. Motivated by the need for a coherent view, this survey examines four recent peer-reviewed studies that together span multimodal COVID-19 diagnosis, privacy-preserving learning on encrypted medical images, graph-refined semi-supervised pathology classification, and an AI-enabled mobile application for personalized healthcare management and doctor recommendation. Using a structured narrative methodology, the reviewed studies are classified into a five-category taxonomy, compared along technical dimensions, healthcare capabilities, and reported limitations, and synthesized into a layered view that treats imaging, multimodal fusion, privacy preservation, label-efficient learning, and personalization as complementary layers of intelligent healthcare rather than independent technologies. The synthesis indicates that each study advances one layer under its own experimental setting, and that none addresses privacy, label efficiency, multimodality, explainability, and clinical validation together. Recurring gaps include limited clinical validation, dataset constraints, unquantified generalization across institutions, privacy–performance trade-offs, and inconsistent evaluation protocols that prevent direct numerical comparison. Future directions include privacy-preserving multimodal learning, reduced reliance on annotations, explainable and robust models, integration of imaging with clinical records, and multi-site clinical validation. This review is not exhaustive, and no new experiments are presented.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for medical image analysis is increasingly being developed for low-resource settings, where specialist expertise, imaging equipment, labelled data, and computing resources may be limited. We systematically reviewed 189 studies published between January 2021 and January 2026 to examine how these constraints relate to imaging modalities, clinical applications, and AI methods in low-resource settings. Each study was also assessed against 15 criteria adapted from the FUTURE-AI principles for trustworthy AI. Shortages of clinical expertise were the most common constraint, and portable or lower-cost imaging was widely used. Transfer learning was the most frequent technical strategy (59%), followed by data augmentation (54%) and efficient model design (36%). Medical-image pretraining and self-supervised learning were each used in 4% of studies, and model compression in 3%. Applications were concentrated in retinal disease, pulmonary disease, antenatal care, parasitic diseases, and cervical screening. Beyond these technical and clinical patterns, the trustworthy AI assessment showed a clear gap between documenting how systems were developed and demonstrating how they performed under relevant local conditions. Subgroup performance was evaluated in 24% of studies, intended users or realistic working conditions in 25%, and model explanations with intended users in 4%. Consistent with this gap, among 15 studies that reported the same model and metric during development and in the local setting, 12 performed worse locally. Future research should prioritise representative local evaluation, intended-user assessment, demonstrated resource suitability, and reproducible research practices.

documents.abstract: Shade selection continues to be an important factor of esthetic success in restorative and prosthetic dentistry.The limitations of traditional optical shade matching-subjective perception, light variability, and metamerism-lead to inconsistent results and unhappy patients.Although instrumental techniques like colorimeters and spectrophotometers increased reproducibility, they are still expensive and technique-sensitive.Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have become revolutionary techniques in recent years for automating and standardizing dental shade matching through the analysis of optical and image-based data.Under controlled conditions, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Support Vector Machines (SVMs), and fuzzy logic systems have shown potential accuracy in tooth shade prediction that is comparable to instrumental approaches.The underlying principles of color science are described, current algorithms and approaches are assessed, and their clinical viability, limitations, and future prospects are discussed in this narrative review, which also synthesizes information from recent research on AI applications in dental shade matching.Prior to clinical translation, problems including dataset bias, illumination standardization, device calibration, and regulatory validation must be resolved, notwithstanding AI's great potential for objective, repeatable, and easily accessible color assessment.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education; however, evidence of its research and application in Ecuador remains fragmented. We systematically reviewed the internationally indexed literature on AI in Ecuadorian higher education. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched for peer-reviewed publications from 2015 to 2025. Of the 271 unique records screened, 62 studies met the eligibility criteria; they were appraised using design-specific instruments (MMAT 2018, PROBAST) and analyzed through thematic synthesis across eight axes. The corpus concentrates on 2024–2025 (71%) and is dominated by learning analytics (16 studies) and generative AI (14 studies), followed by perception studies (10 studies). Reported benefits—early warning, efficiency, assessment support, and skill development—rest on technical performance, usability, and satisfaction rather than on measured learning or institutional gains. Persistent challenges include infrastructure constraints, uneven digital competencies, ethical and privacy concerns, and methodologically fragile local evidence; 30 of the 59 appraised studies were rated as having high concern. Ethics, governance, and academic integrity were rarely the primary research objects (two of 62 studies), although 28 raised them as secondary findings. This review derives a research agenda prioritizing governance, pedagogical theorization, methodological rigor, and outcome evidence.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a general-purpose set of computational methods that is increasingly embedded in scientific research and technological systems. This critical narrative review evaluates the principal roles of AI across scientific discovery, medicine, environmental and space science, manufacturing, software engineering, cybersecurity and communication networks, while distinguishing demonstrated capabilities from claims that remain context dependent. The review also examines conceptual differences between task-bounded AI and human intelligence, and considers human–AI collaboration as a practical design problem rather than a contest between interchangeable forms of intelligence. Literature was selected through transparent live scholarly searching and verification, with an emphasis on peer-reviewed evidence, primary studies for prominent performance claims and authoritative governance sources. The evidence indicates that AI is especially useful where large, high-dimensional or multimodal data must be classified, modelled or searched, and where repeated decisions can be evaluated against explicit performance criteria. Examples include protein-structure prediction, anomaly detection, remote-sensing analysis, autonomous planetary navigation, smart manufacturing and cyber-threat analysis. Nevertheless, high benchmark performance does not automatically establish clinical utility, causal understanding, robustness under distribution shift, safety or equitable deployment. Major cross-cutting limitations include data quality, representativeness, opaque decision processes, evaluation leakage, infrastructure requirements, environmental cost, cybersecurity vulnerabilities and uneven institutional capacity. Responsible integration therefore requires task-specific validation, human oversight, traceability, monitoring and governance proportional to potential harm. Future progress will depend less on simply increasing model scale than on improving scientific validity, causal and mechanistic integration, reproducibility, context-sensitive evaluation and access in lower-resource settings. AI is best understood as an enabling technology whose scientific and social value depends on the quality of the evidence, institutions and human judgement surrounding its use.

documents.abstract: The study investigated Artificial Intelligence in University Education: Exploring the Attitudes of Science Education Students in Makurdi, Nigeria. The study employed a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 670 (374 males and 296 females) 400-level science education students of Rev. Fr. Moses Orshio Adasu University and Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University for the 2025/2026 academic session. A sample size of 237 (102 males and 135 females) students was selected using purposive sampling technique. The instrument for data collection was "Students' Attitude toward Artificial Intelligence Integration Questionnaire (SAAIIQ)." Validated by two experts in Science Education. Cronbach's Alpha was used to determine the reliability coefficient of the instrument, and the reliability coefficient obtained was 0.85. Two research questions and one hypothesis was tested. Descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation were used for answering the research questions, while inferential statistics of independent t-test was used for testing the hypothesis at 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that science education students exhibited a positive attitude toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 3.14. The study also found no significant difference between the attitudes of male and female students toward Al integration. Students demonstrated a moderate perception toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 2.98. The study concluded that students generally accept the use of AI in university, adequate infrastructure, institutional support, and training are necessary for its effective implementation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to modern virus detection, particularly as metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) expands diagnostic and surveillance capabilities beyond targeted assays. This paper reviews how AI supports virus detection across three interconnected levels. The metagenomic layer forms the technical core of the review, while the clinical and population sections examine how sequence-level AI outputs are translated into patient-level and public-health decision support. At the metagenomic level, AI addresses key bottlenecks caused by fragmented assemblies and weak homology signals. Foundation-model approaches such as ViraLM leverage pretrained genome representations to improve viral contig discrimination under short-contig conditions, whereas LucaProt integrates sequence- and structure-informed learning to detect highly divergent RNA viruses via RdRP (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase)-focused discovery. At the clinical level, targeted molecular tests remain effective when the suspected pathogen is known, while mNGS provides a complementary, hypothesis-free approach that can broaden etiological investigation in complex infections when laboratories apply appropriate quality control and clinicians interpret results in context. At the population level, early warning systems combine heterogeneous data sources (epidemiological, open-source, digital, environmental, and wastewater signals) with AI methods to enhance outbreak detection and forecasting. Across all levels, robust contamination control, transparent reporting, external validation, and standardized interpretation criteria determine real-world value. Overall, hybrid pipelines that integrate molecular evidence, clinical metadata, and population-scale surveillance within governed, reproducible workflows are likely to provide the greatest impact.

documents.abstract: Background: Benign and malignant laryngeal lesions frequently present with dysphonia, making clinical differentiation based on voice characteristics alone challenging. Acoustic voice analysis provides objective measurements of vocal function, while artificial intelligence (AI) may identify complex acoustic patterns that are difficult to recognize using conventional parameters. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of an AI-assisted acoustic voice analysis system in differentiating benign from malignant laryngeal lesions using clinically characterized voice recordings. Materials and Methods: A prospective diagnostic validation study was conducted among adults with laryngeal lesions confirmed by endoscopic and histopathological assessment with ethics committee approval and written informed consent. Standardized sustained-vowel and connected-speech recordings were subjected to acoustic analysis. Fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR), cepstral peak prominence (CPP), spectral parameters and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients were extracted. Machine-learning classifiers including logistic regression, random forest and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) .Histopathological diagnosis was the reference standard. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) where estimable from the available model outputs. Results: Among 120 participants, 78 had benign and 42 had malignant lesions. The XGBoost model yielded an AUC of 0.91. Based on the reported confusion matrix, sensitivity was 88.1% (95% CI 75.0–94.8%), specificity 84.6% (95% CI 75.0–91.0%), PPV 75.5% (95% CI 61.9–85.4%), NPV 93.0% (95% CI 84.6–97.0%), accuracy 85.8% (95% CI 78.5–91.0%) and F1 score 0.81. Random forest and logistic regression yielded AUCs of 0.86 and 0.82, respectively. Conclusion: AI-assisted acoustic voice analysis has potential as a non-invasive adjunctive approach for differentiating benign and malignant laryngeal lesions. The reported performance reflects internal validation in a single-centre cohort and should not be regarded as evidence of clinical diagnostic effectiveness until confirmed in an external cohort. Its role should presently be considered complementary to laryngoscopic examination and histopathological diagnosis. Larger prospective, multicentre and externally validated datasets are required before routine clinical implementation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping English language education through generative chatbots, automated writing evaluation, intelligent tutoring systems, speech-recognition applications, adaptive learning environments, and AI-supported feedback. This PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesizes recent international and Uzbekistan-specific evidence on the effectiveness of AI-based tools in improving English language proficiency among university students. The review focuses on writing, speaking, reading, listening, vocabulary, feedback, motivation, engagement, and learner autonomy. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews generally report positive effects, particularly for productive skills and individualized feedback, but they also reveal substantial heterogeneity across technologies, intervention duration, learner profiles, and research designs. Evidence on ChatGPT and related generative AI tools suggests benefits for idea generation, revision, conversational practice, and autonomous learning, while highlighting risks related to inaccurate information, overreliance, academic integrity, privacy, and uneven AI literacy. Emerging studies from Uzbekistan confirm strong interest in AI-supported language learning and indicate potential benefits for writing and vocabulary development, although local evidence remains smaller and methodologically less mature than the international literature. The review concludes that AI is most effective when integrated into structured pedagogy, combined with teacher guidance, and supported by explicit AI literacy and ethical-use practices.

Artificial intelligence-enabled computer vision can increase the frequency and spatial coverage of food inspection, but high predictive accuracy does not establish reliable production decisions. This critical narrative review examines the evidence connecting image measurements with grading, rejection, and process control. Representative studies across produce, grains and nuts, meat and seafood, microbiology, and packaging are compared by sensing modality, reference endpoint, validation unit, and operational action. The synthesis distinguishes visible quality from specific hazards, prepared defects from natural variation, and image-level performance from verified product outcomes. An author-proposed evidence map organizes analytical feasibility, independent-sample testing, operational challenges, external transfer, and prospective impact as partly independent dimensions. It is unvalidated and is not a readiness score or regulatory standard. Task-dependent reporting considerations address uncertainty, prevalence, false rejection, and abstention. Safety-related uses require separate hazard-specific validation, sampling, and acceptance criteria. Process integration additionally requires acquisition-to-actuation testing, accepted-product verification, and controlled updates. The purposive evidence base cannot establish field-wide effectiveness or rank modalities. Research priorities include traceable datasets, mechanistic challenges, and prospective intervention studies. Progress toward closed-loop control should be judged by stable measurements and demonstrated effects on defined product and process outcomes within a stated operating domain.

documents.abstract: Climate change, increasing food demand, and resource constraints are accelerating the transition from conventional precision agriculture toward smart, autonomous, and climate-resilient agricultural systems. Artificial intelligence (AI), foundation models, digital twins (DTs), the Internet of Things (IoT), remote sensing, edge–cloud computing, and big data analytics are emerging as key technologies for data-driven agricultural management. This review critically evaluates recent advances in AI-driven intelligent agriculture, with emphasis on machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI (XAI), generative and agentic AI, multimodal foundation models, and digital twins, together with the sensing and computing infrastructures required for their deployment. Relevant literature was identified using keywords related to AI, foundation models, digital twins, IoT, precision agriculture, and climate-resilient agriculture, with emphasis on recent peer-reviewed studies addressing technological applications, performance, limitations, challenges, and future prospects. The selected literature was critically synthesized to identify technological trends, knowledge gaps, and emerging research opportunities. The review highlights that the greatest potential of intelligent agriculture lies in integrating heterogeneous data from sensors, UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles), satellites, weather systems, field operations, and agricultural knowledge to support context-aware prediction, decision-making, and autonomous action. However, data quality, model generalizability, explainability, interoperability, cybersecurity, computational requirements, and large-scale field validation remain major challenges. This review further develops an integrated perspective connecting AI, foundation models, multimodal data infrastructures, digital twins, and autonomous agricultural systems within a unified cyber-physical ecosystem. Future priorities include trustworthy AI, agentic decision-making, semantic interoperability, federated learning, continuous learning, and self-learning digital twins toward Agriculture 6.0.

Groundwater serves as a vital resource for drinking and household needs across rural communities in Maharashtra's Chandrapur District. This research was conducted to examine the physicochemical properties of local groundwater and determine its viability for human consumption and daily use. Water samples gathered from various rural sites in the district underwent laboratory testing for key parameters using standard analytical methods, encompassing color, calcium, chloride, electrical conductivity, fluoride, magnesium, nitrate, pH, total dissolved solids, total alkalinity, total hardness, turbidity, iron, and sulfate, with results benchmarked against established drinking-water standards. Furthermore, the study highlights geographic variations in water quality driven by regional geology and human factors such as farming practices, domestic wastewater, and improper waste disposal. This evaluation pinpoints specific water parameters and locations requiring focused public water management, ultimately emphasizing the necessity of consistent monitoring, proper treatment, source safeguarding, and contamination control to preserve safe and sustainable groundwater supplies in rural Chandrapur.

Online examinations provide flexibility and accessibility for students and educational institutions, but maintaining academic integrity in remote assessment environments remains a major challenge due to limited direct supervision. Traditional examination methods may not effectively identify impersonation, unauthorized materials, suspicious movements, or attempts to access external resources during an examination. To address these challenges, this paper presents a Smart Proctoring System for Online Examinations that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), computer vision, audio monitoring, and web technologies to support automated examination supervision.

Walking sequences reveal human-interpretable attributes related to body structure, posture, and motion. Gait attribute recognition provides a concrete route to fine-grained gait understanding by predicting these attributes. However, existing benchmarks provide limited fine-grained annotations, while classifier-based gait attribute recognition methods typically represent candidate classes through learned output weights rather than directly matching visual evidence with textual class representations. To address the annotation gap, we present RA-GAR, a large-scale, richly annotated multimodal benchmark for gait attribute recognition, containing 1,001 subjects, 242,729 walking sequences, and annotations for 15 static and motion gait attributes. We further propose Gait-VL, an attribute-centric vision-language alignment framework that recognizes gait attributes by matching attribute-specific multi-frame visual evidence with textual class prototypes. On the visual side, attribute-specific learnable queries aggregate RGB features across spatial locations and frames into per-attribute visual embeddings. On the language side, diverse descriptions expanded by a large language model are combined with context about relevant body regions to construct textual class prototypes. Beyond attribute recognition, we evaluate the transferability of the attribute-pretrained visual encoder by using it to replace generic upstream large vision models in identityoriented gait recognition pipelines; attribute pre-training uses no identity classification or metric-learning objectives. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art attribute recognition performance on RA-GAR and consistent improvements in downstream identity recognition across multiple pipelines and benchmarks, supporting the effectiveness and transferability of attribute-centric gait representation learning.

This study explores the integration of Large Language Model (LLM)-based Automated Essay Scoring (AES) into classroom writing assessment within an Intensive English Program (IEP). Using a corpus of 46 multi-draft capstone essays written by international students in an Academic Literacies course, the study evaluates the performance of two OpenAI models (GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-5.1) against rubric-based human instructor scores. Essays were scored twice by each model under controlled temperature settings to evaluate linear association, systematic bias, inter-model consistency, and performance-band agreement. Findings reveal that while both LLM scores maintain moderate positive correlations with human ratings (r = .44 for GPT-4.1-mini; r = .49 for GPT-5.1), both models exhibit systematic negative bias, scoring essays an average of 13 points lower than the human instructor. However, the two models demonstrate strong inter-model consistency (r = .84) and an exact band-level agreement of 87%. Qualitative analysis of the holistic comments shows that LLMs focus on global discourse features but lack sensitivity to local, process-oriented classroom constructs. The results suggest that uncalibrated zero-shot LLMs serve better as formative diagnostic tools than autonomous grading systems.Keywords: Automated essay scoring, Large Language Models, GPT-5, L2 academic writing, multi-method validity, formative assessment.

Artificial intelligence has become a central pillar of institutional management in Nigerian higher education, processing massive volumes of student data for admissions, predictive analytics, and attendance management. However, this data-intensive transformation operates under the strict oversight of the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) of 2023. Despite these legal obligations, empirical evidence reveals a systemic governance deficit, characterized by bundled consent, unlawful cross-border data transfers, and automated decision-making without human oversight. This project aimed to design, develop, and evaluate an Automated NDPA Compliance Toolkit to systematically detect and remediate compliance violations within artificial intelligence-driven Student Management Systems. Design Science Research was adopted as the primary methodology, supported by documentary analysis and comparative technology assessment. The developed toolkit features a three-layer architecture utilizing Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and React.js, operationalizing the NDPA into 25 executable checks across six compliance modules. Testing was conducted using a simulated non-compliant institution and a compliant control system. The toolkit successfully identified all planted violations in the non-compliant system, assigning a compliance health index of 12 percent, while accurately passing all checks for the compliant system with a 100 percent score. The confusion matrix indicated 100 percent detection accuracy and specificity. The findings establish that software can effectively bridge the gap between statutory requirements and practical implementation by translating legal provisions into verifiable technical controls.
