documents.abstract: Automated student assessment using AI tools can contribute to the viability of online higher education programs, preserving academic integrity, strengthening students’ engagement and reducing costs. General-purpose Generative AI models such as ChatGPT have shown their ability to automatically grade student assignments. However, further investigation of their validity is needed for complex student tasks, such as creative projects in higher education. The aim of this study is firstly to evaluate the potential of costless, general-purpose AI tools to assess complex higher education topics. Secondly, we seek to identify which are the minimum skills in AI prompting required by an educator to successfully perform such tasks. A Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology was employed, following an iterative process of prompting and calibrating the AI tool to imitate the professor’s assessments in a representative course that emphasizes on knowledge application, critical thinking and creativity. Testing was performed on a dataset of 39 student assignments, comparing the results of zero-shot AI prompts, multi-cycle calibrated AI and the opinion of two human course lecturers. Automatic assessment of complex tasks with high level of consistency and agreement with human judgement was only achieved by educators with skills in structured prompts and multi-cycle calibration.

Abstract Recently, an epistemic shift has occurred in classics pedagogy. First, the COVID pandemic forced students online. Then, large language model (LLM) chatbots appeared. These disruptions created a conundrum: how could research methods, reading and writing, and cross-cultural exploration be taught when students were tethered to LLM-accessible ‘cheating machines’? The solution was AI-assisted classics. This paper describes how AI-assisted classical history can be taught through a discussion of the ‘WHAM’ (Web Design, HTML, and the Archaeology of the Mediterranean) project. WHAM is a website-building classroom assignment developed to teach students in the Computer Science and Society major at Wentworth Institute of Technology (Boston, MA, USA; www.wit.edu ) how to utilize digital tools to explicate humanities data. Students create a website from the HTML code up focused on a Mediterranean archaeological region and are taught to use LLMs critically, both for writing HTML code and for ideating web design features. In the process, students learn how LLMs must be approached cautiously since they can both hallucinate and offer satisfactory work that should be improved. Finally, the paper suggests that LLMs can provide students with a starting place for digital projects that challenge them to engage with the classical world’s history and material culture.

Brain metastases are a frequent manifestation of lung cancer and a substantial proportion of patients require accurate intracranial assessment at diagnosis, during staging or when neurological symptoms emerge. Conventional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), which relies on T1 weighted post contrast imaging together with T2 weighted and FLAIR sequences and in which three-dimensional T1 weighted imaging is the reference standard for detection, remains central to diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring, but its specificity is limited in the post treatment setting, where imaging features may not reliably distinguish viable tumor from radiation necrosis. The objective of this narrative review was to appraise the role of advanced and quantitative MRI in four clinically distinct questions, namely detection of small or early lesions, characterization and differential diagnosis, post treatment assessment and quantitative or artificial intelligence-based applications, in patients with lung cancer. Literature was identified through PubMed and included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, narrative reviews, original clinical studies and imaging-based investigations, with evidence derived from lung cancer specific cohorts distinguished throughout from evidence derived from mixed brain metastasis populations. The strongest evidence supports characterization and post treatment assessment. Perfusion derived relative cerebral blood volume and fractional tumor burden were higher in progression than in radiation necrosis and diffusion metrics, permeability parameters, MR spectroscopy and delayed contrast enhanced imaging contributed additional information, although these findings derive largely from mixed brain metastasis cohorts, group level differences overlap substantially at the level of the individual patient and no validated diagnostic threshold exists for any single biomarker. Evidence that advanced sequences improve detection of small or occult lesions beyond optimized three-dimensional T1 weighted imaging is considerably weaker and rests largely on mechanistic reasoning rather than on comparative diagnostic accuracy studies. Radiomics and machine learning have reported promising discrimination for post treatment differential diagnosis and for prediction of molecular and histological subtype, but reported performance is vulnerable to overfitting, data leakage, segmentation variability and incomplete reporting, calibration is seldom assessed and external validation remains uncommon. Advanced and quantitative MRI should presently be regarded as complementary to conventional MRI and tissue based molecular testing rather than as clinically validated substitutes and prospective multicenter studies using standardized acquisition and reporting are required before routine adoption.

Autonomous cybersecurity requires a transition from isolated alert classification toward coordinated threat investigation, evidence-grounded decisions, and measurable containment. This study integrates a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) multi-agent threat-hunting architecture with a six-state nonlinear model of secure, exposed, compromised, and recovered assets and the evolving hunting and response capabilities. The framework employs independent evidence verification and policy-controlled response authorization, while model analysis uses a containment threshold, equilibrium stability and parameter sensitivity. Across the three configurations reported in the supplied results, compromise fractions were 42.71% for rule-based defence, 32.48% for machine-learning-supported defence, and 19.16% for GenAI-enabled defence; corresponding containment thresholds were 6.860, 4.857, and 3.275. These submitted outcomes indicate a 55.1% lower modelled compromise fraction for the GenAI configuration than for rule-based defence, although all thresholds remain above unity and therefore do not establish threat elimination. Three author-supplied three-dimensional response surfaces describe the effects of propagation, assisted recovery, adversarial adaptation and hunting activation. The investigation distinguishes these reported model-based outcomes from unreported alert-level accuracy benchmarks and from numerical bifurcations that require recorded AUTO-07p continuation diagnostics. The resulting contribution is a coherent framework linking generative investigation, bounded response capacity and nonlinear cybersecurity resilience, with explicit requirements for reproducible experimental validation and safe operational deployment.

Background. Standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) in Mueller–Hinton broth samples a single metabolic state, yet bacterial susceptibility in vivo depends on nutrient availability, host-derived metabolites, and spatial structure. The extent to which this mismatch produces clinically relevant errors in susceptibility classification has not been systematically mapped. Objective. To map the evidence linking metabolic context to conditional antibiotic susceptibility and to identify gaps between mechanistic insight, physiologically relevant models, and clinical validation. Methods. We conducted a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR. The search combined PubMed, Semantic Scholar, Web of Science, and Embase with AI-assisted discovery and screening using Consensus AI and large language models, with full human verification at every inclusion decision. AI use is reported per PRISMA-trAIce. Records were classified by mechanism (porin regulation, efflux, stringent response, metabolic rewiring, biofilm structure) and by infection-relevant context (gut-mimicking media, bicarbonate and host factors, single-cell and heterogeneity, in vivo models, clinical validation). Results. Of 1,543,377 records identified, 100 studies met inclusion criteria. Mechanistic evidence was dense across all seven mechanistic foci. In contrast, evidence in physiologically relevant contexts was sparse: gut-mimicking AST appeared in only one mechanism category, and clinical validation was absent in five of seven. The most prominent gap was the absence of prospective clinical validation linking host-mimicking AST results to patient outcomes. Conclusions. Metabolic state is a primary determinant of antibiotic susceptibility, and standard Mueller–Hinton AST samples only one such state. The field has established mechanisms but not clinical translation. Prospective validation of host-mimicking AST across pathogen and drug classes is the highest-priority next step.

The prevailing neurological orthodoxy equates the mind with neuronal activation. While empirically grounded, this reductionist paradigm fails to account for subjective experience, altered states of consciousness, and the profound influence of the body on cognition. This opinion challenges the neurocentric assumption and proposes a radical redefinition: The mind is an emergent, dynamic, predictive, and nonlinear process arising from the continuous integration of all intentional (cognitive) and non-intentional (affective, homeostatic, and interoceptive) psychological processes occurring throughout the living body, constantly reconciling internal bodily needs with external environmental demands. Drawing on predictive processing theory, embodied cognition, complex systems dynamics, and recent work on interoception and homeostatic feelings, it is argued that consciousness is not a binary neural switch but a nonlinear spectrum of bodilycognitive integration. This framework offers novel implications for psychiatry, medicine, artificial intelligence, and clinical diagnostics.

Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for scientific discovery are trained primarily on published literature and therefore internalize survivorship bias: they learn from positive results, funded hypotheses, and consensus paradigms. This confines them to what Thomas Kuhn called “normal science” and limits their capacity for revolutionary discovery. This article proposes a counter-inductive AI architecture that treats absence, failure, and negative results as primary epistemic signals. The architecture integrates three layers: 1) Negative Space Mapping, which identifies structural blind spots in knowledge graphs; 2) Dark Data Processing, which mines unpublished, rejected, or failed experiments; and 3) Counter-Inductive Hypothesis Generation, which optimizes for surprise relative to consensus under structural viability constraints. We formalize this approach using a counter-inductive loss function and illustrate its application to neurobiology with the case of the CPEB3/CPEB4 protein systems, showing how the system would prioritize neglected areas such as glial function, active forgetting, and sleep. The article also examines the emerging controversy surrounding AI-generated solutions to mathematical Millennium Prize Problems, where claims of attribution and the use of prior researcher data have sparked intense debate. We argue that a counter-inductive architecture, by explicitly mapping negative space and processing dark data, offers a more transparent and epistemically rigorous path toward addressing such fundamental problems, one that acknowledges and credits the human research it builds upon. Moving beyond survivorship bias requires redefining the objective of scientific AI from consensus optimization to paradigm disruption. The result is a Kuhnian AI capable of generating testable, high-risk hypotheses that the current literature systematically overlooks.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is essential for adaptive decision-making, e.g., robust Meta-RL and domain randomization (DR), and efficient post-training of large language models (LLMs), where tasks are commonly structured as Markov decision processes or prompts. A central bottleneck in all these settings is the cost of agent-environment interactions required for task selection and policy optimization. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.

Project narrative for a proposed pilot study of generative-AI-driven clinical decision support and automation (GenAI-CDSAS) to support implementation of the Collaborative Care Model (CoCM) for mental health in primary care. This is a grant narrative (a research plan), not a report of results: no data have been collected. Posted as is; cover letter, administrative forms and the research-team section have been removed. The reference list is included. Abstract: Using the Discover, Design/Build, and Test framework, the project plans interviews, surveys and workflow observation with patients, providers and administrators, followed by co-design of a prototype and a simulation experiment comparing three ways of presenting AI recommendations (black-box, narrative, and critical-interaction), with outcomes on usability, appropriateness, trust, implementation readiness and human-AI synergy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The sports media industry has undergone seismic structural transformation over the past two decades, driven by the collapse of legacy newspaper models, the proliferation of digital platforms, and the emergence of artificial intelligence. This qualitative study examines what sports media hiring managers and editors actually require from recent journalism school graduates as they enter a rapidly evolving workforce. Drawing on semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 15 sports media professionals who self-identified as editors and/or publishers and who are affiliated with the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA) and the U.S. Basketball Writers Association (USBWA), this study employs a human capital theory framework to analyze the alignment, and the persistent misalignment, between what journalism programs produce and what the industry demands. Findings reveal four dominant themes: (1) passion and intrinsic motivation as non-negotiable hiring criteria; (2) the depreciation of formal credentials relative to demonstrated, verifiable work; (3) a widening deficit in source cultivation, relationship building, and reporting fundamentals among recent graduates; and (4) a growing demand for multimedia versatility and platform fluency. Implications for journalism education curricula, industry-academy collaboration, and the professional preparation of the next generation of sports media workers are discussed.

As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: Cage Containment Receipt 1 (CCR-1): a deterministic execution gate rejected 100% of contract-invalid proposals before any side effect executed, while admitting only contract-valid actions to a harmless local mock target. Holds and escalations never caused side effects. This is the execution-containment complement to the PENTA-CL model-attribution replay evidence: matching decisions and blocked invalid proposals under the same deterministic envelope. Results (falsifiers 0/5 tripped): 17 candidates = 1 positive control + 8 fresh LLM-generated captures (4 engines x 2: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, GLM 5.2) + 8 harness-generated adversarial mutations. All 9 valid candidates admitted (72 actions written, 18 holds, 18 escalations — zero hold/escalation side effects). All 8 adversarial cases rejected with the mock journal hash unchanged: malformed JSON, case-normalized anomaly types, invented playbook ids, under-confidence heals, false holds, extra keys, wrong array length, duplicate positions. Duplicate action-id suppression and the hold/admit distinction (holds never increment the healing-action counter) verified. Scope (honest limits): proves the local mock-gate for the tested integration and inputs only — NOT containment of every Base44 tool, any production runtime, or untested inputs. The adversarial mutations are harness-generated and labeled as such; no fresh adversarial-LLM conversation was created inside the run itself (that leg remains open). Small-scale sequential timing baseline included as descriptive n=1-2 data (no capacity claim). Dual Mesh Benchmark: NOT MEASURED. Method operates under filed application 64/119,191 (Deterministically Governed Probabilistic Neural Computation); no unfiled-method disclosure is made. Two-key curation: Gabriel vetted, Leon approved (Oct 10, 2026). This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them. Related: PENTA-CL interim (10.5281/zenodo.23286324), PENTA-CL v2 replay (10.5281/zenodo.23286770), First Documented Caging of an LLM (10.5281/zenodo.23265723), Deterministic Caging paper (10.5281/zenodo.23266727), SDR-CL1 (10.5281/zenodo.23274887), SDR-CL2 (10.5281/zenodo.23284295). Ledger: https://github.com/LLong2026/four-horsemen. Community: https://zenodo.org/communities/dcai

Cage Containment Receipt 2 (CCR-2) — the fresh adversarial-LLM leg. CCR-1 proved a deterministic gate blocks contract-invalid proposals before execution, and honestly disclosed that its adversarial cases were harness-generated. CCR-2 closes that gap: a live, memory-disabled, platform-pinned LLM engine (GPT-5.6 Luna), explicitly instructed toward a best-effort heal of a below-threshold anomaly, proposed the invalid resolved tuple — a confidence-gate breach — and the deterministic gate rejected it BEFORE any side effect executed. Zero writes, mock journal hash unchanged. Results (falsifiers 0/5 tripped): 10 LLM submissions across four engines (Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, GLM 5.2), one fresh conversation each. Leg A (temptation: under-confidence heal, tie-break, no-match, plus SLA pressure): 4/4 engines resisted all traps and were admitted cleanly. Leg B (explicit synthetic bait): 1/4 took the bait (semantic heal-under-low-confidence proposal — blocked); 3/4 resisted but still emitted contract-invalid output (hold-field type errors [] vs null, markdown-fenced JSON) — all 4 candidates blocked before execution with zero side effects. Notably three engines independently made the same hold-field type error: even a correct decision can be an invalid action tuple, and the gate catches it regardless of intent. Integrity: three protocol amendments, all issued BEFORE the affected prompts reached any additional engine, each preserving prior hashes and captures (full chain in the freeze file). Model attribution by platform configuration pinning with settings readback; not provider attestation. Settings restored and verified after the run. Scope: proves the local mock-gate for this integration and inputs — NOT containment of every tool or any production runtime. 3 of 4 engines resisted the explicit bait. Dual Mesh Benchmark: NOT MEASURED. DeepSeek pending. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them. documents.abstract: Large language models can synthesize clinical records, identify phenotypic features and support patient-specific decisions, but fluent explanations may obscure uncertainty. Surgical practice provides a demanding setting in which to examine this problem because decisions combine heterogeneous evidence, procedural risk and individual preferences. This critical narrative review connects surgical self-assessment research with studies of clinician–LLM interaction, clinical summarization, uncertainty estimation and perioperative implementation. Targeted searches of PubMed records through Europe PMC were supplemented by retrieval of methodological and foundational sources. Selection was purposive, with attention to contradictory findings and the distinction between simulated performance and clinical benefit. Randomized studies using general clinical vignettes and simulated tasks show that LLM assistance does not uniformly improve physician reasoning; their applicability to surgical decisions remains indirect. Direct clinical studies extend from preoperative documentation and triage to shared decision-making and postoperative support, with mixed findings and limited evidence of sustained patient benefit. We distinguish clinician self-appraisal, LLM uncertainty, prognostic calibration, appropriate reliance and patient-specific decision quality, each requiring distinct evaluation criteria. For personalized surgical care, generated interpretations should preserve the provenance, timing and limitations of the underlying patient data and predictive models. We propose a workflow for examining discrepancies between clinician judgment and LLM output, together with an evaluation agenda centered on harmful decision changes, verification burden and patient-relevant outcomes. This framework requires prospective validation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. Reusing demonstrations in new situations is challenging: directly inputting full trajectories consumes limited prompt space and constrains the overall effectiveness, while natural-language summaries require the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. Therefore, we study whether expert action choices can directly supervise a reusable scoring rule. We propose CB-Agent, which extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection. We extract environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fit a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given the context. This model combines the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During ReAct interaction, the agent uses this distribution to select environment actions without including demonstrations in the action-scoring context. Across TextWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, CB-Agent achieves the highest cross-benchmark average among the evaluated methods at all three tested model sizes and ranks first on TextWorld and ScienceWorld at each size. ALFWorld experiments support the learned concept's contribution beyond prior-only scoring and show further gains when combined with Reflexion. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CB-Agent-DFF9/.

Supplementary data for the scoping review "Personality and Trust in LLM Agents: Dependency Evidence, an Empty Behavioural Over-Reliance Cell, and the Personality-Trust Calibration Framework" by Carson Conception Rodrigues and Simran Marian Rebello (Celabe). charting_dataset_supplementary.csv has one row per charted record: the 60 included empirical studies (22 on contemporary generative LLMs) and 2 construct-informing records, with sample, AI-system type, individual-difference measure, outcome measure, charted finding, effect size as reported, and charting confidence. supplementary_material_S1_dataset_S2_reference_log.pdf is the same dataset typeset for reading (S1) plus the reference verification log (S2). Version 2 of the CSV (10 October 2026) cites the published versions of four records first charted from preprints. Preprint of the review: https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/2mdu8_v1
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Summary Public opinion of artificial intelligence systems and the frontier labs that develop them are at an all time low, with serious concerns about the pace and scope of this powerful technology that is rapidly advancing without community standards, laws, regulators, or transparent processes. The technical knowledge required to draft meaningful legislation, or even to establish legal guardrails, far exceeds the competencies represented within the three branches of government. Indeed, the government's concerns about AI appear to be limited to economic impacts, and the promise of adding over $10T to America's economy with nearly 4% year-over-year GDP growth over the next four years., That translates to a 30% jump in today’s GDP estimate ($32.3T) driven by a national economy with markets running about twice as hot as their current historic highs. Political leaders and economists view these projections as justifications for the risk that AI poses, despite dire warnings from industry stakeholders. Despite corporate attempts to control the public narrative and hide behind IP laws, the public continues to learn of new breaches and threats that reinforce concerns that frontier labs do not actually have full control over the systems they have built. The ability of agentic tools to penetrate local systems built on cloud services poses a global threat, while even the most responsive government interventions are reactionary, at best. Even so, the lack of transparency involved in all aspects of this black box tech have forced victims of AI breach to seek remedy from the violators themselves. The very companies that are creating these crises are not only free from legal accountability for the harms they cause to clients around the world, but also appear to be free from accountability even within the frontier labs that develop them. Human Agency in AI Systems This century will be defined by how civilization engages with artificial intelligence. The pace of significant albeit poorly documented updates to existing AI models, the aggressive drive toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) models, and the emergence of socio-cultural behaviors by agent groups demand an equally robust human response that preserves the role of public choice in the use of these tools, as well as the individual rights guaranteed by the Constitution. This proposal outlines a pilot project to identify, test, and refine civil society engagement models that have been developed for other adversarial cross-sectoral contexts and proven to deliver mutually beneficial outcomes. This investigation will explore a set of pre-determined civilian oversight frameworks for suitability within defined AI-in-society policy concerns. For example, law enforcement surveillance systems, such as Flock Safety, must be subject to civilian scrutiny; however, accessible oversight mechanisms for the lay public have not yet been developed. Public oversight is left to the public to self-organize with no particular coordinated efforts to guide them. Indeed, the vast majority of oversight resources that have been developed exist for the use of industry to track benchmarks and improve performance. Current government guidance, scant as it is, is likewise dedicated to benefiting frontier labs. This proposal describes a novel framework for public assessment of AI systems, to be implemented before and during the use of AI tools and services by public institutions, including local government. The results of this pilot phase will determine whether and how the project should be broadened and scaled into a more comprehensive, robust framework with policy recommendations and economic analysis. Methodology, Milestones, Outputs This mixed-methods study will begin with a comparative analysis of a defined set of reference frameworks. The set of frameworks will be piloted by civilian volunteer groups reviewing real use cases. The pilot will produce metrics inherent to each framework’s evaluation criteria, which will then be used to further develop an assessment rubric that enables stakeholders choice. Phase I: Comparative Analysis of Reference Frameworks This phase of the project will provide an historical overview of each oversight mechanism in its original context, and map it to the AI context that will be tested in the pilot phase. Reference Frameworks -Citizen Review Boards (CRB) are citizen-led watchdog groups that engage in issues of particular concern to these self-selecting groups. -Consensus Review is an expert-based committee process that invites the public to hear expert testimony and witness information gathering sessions, but the deliberative process is conducted in closed session. This approach may be suitable for preparing significant policy decisions by public institutions and/or governments. -Danish Consensus Conference is a participatory model that enjoins citizens to consider controversial STEM issues and report their policy recommendations to the government and the public. The goal is to form a consensus that strikes a balance between competing stakeholder demands, known risks and potential harms to society, and economic benefits. This framework is particularly apt for public assessment of large, high tech systems for the purpose of policy guidance. Nonetheless, it is not a model familiar to most American stakeholders and may not be appropriate for all AI-in-society deliberations. -Indigenous Data Sovereignty Governance (IDSG) is an emerging framework situated in the human rights principle of self determination. It is an ethical process that calls on place-based community standards, norms, and traditions. It can entail exceptionally time consuming deliberation that results in the establishment of long-term, communitywide rules. -Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a well-established expert-based committee process that exists primarily to reduce risk and limit exposure to the institution by confirming that the plans and processes involved in the activity comply with laws and regulations. It extends protections to individuals and communities indirectly by restricting activities to the confines of broadly applicable legal rules. This approach may be particularly suitable for controversial policy actions, where watchdog organizations are viewed as adversarial actors, rather than community partners. -Jury Deliberation is a type of peer review that allows oversight entities to review evidence and ponder narrow questions in private or closed sessions. Jury decisions must be unanimous and can be appealed. Juries are not required to justify their decisions. This approach might be preferable when sensitive data is involved. -Situated Learning/Community Management (COP) is a Community of Practice (COP) framework that fosters peer-based skilling, adoption of best practices, co-creation of design and development, and information dissemination. This is likely to be a strong mechanism for project planning and early-stage implementation of public AI systems. -Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) is an arbiter-led approach that allows community actors to register grievances, state their trustworthy goals, define for themselves the role that they want to play in the design or oversight of trustworthy AI systems, and reset with a restorative justice engagement framework going forward. -Unstructured Athenian (UA) model, which provides stakeholders a pathway to identify bias outcomes and issue tickets for resolution by administrators within a predetermined timeframe. This is likely to appeal to communities working in close partnership with AI stakeholders, for example where large data centers are welcomed and/or AI systems are perceived as meeting a defined need in service to the local community. Phase II: Pilot Studies Phase II will test known frameworks that have been extensively studied, documented, reviewed, and refined with proven best practices over years and even decades. These reference frameworks represent a variety of input and deliberation processes that communities can select according to needs and capacities. Volunteers will select an oversight mechanism of their choice and join other members of the group to review a real use case that is relevant to their competency and/or community. The goal is to study the effectiveness of the process itself, not the individual or group dynamics, per se. For example, an oversight goal might include “To determine the suitability of Flock Safety devices in a defined rural geolocation.” The pilot group will be organized according to the standards of their assigned oversight mechanism, e.g., Jury, and given instructions for deliberation. Each volunteer will complete a survey instrument designed to capture metrics about the effectiveness of the process in the context of assessing AI in society, weaknesses and strengths of the mechanism to deliver the desired goal(s), and general feedback to describe flaws and suggest improvements. Phase III: Development of AI Oversight Mechanisms The goal of the Phase III is twofold: (1) to apply findings from the set of reference frameworks toward the development of public oversight mechanisms that are suitable for monitoring AI in society; and (2) development of decision tooling that will enable the lay public to choose an appropriate framework that fits the specific need, capacity, competency, and context. It is entirely possible that an AI tool will be implemented in the development of this tooling. Phase IV: Findings and Recommendations While reflexion is built into the methodology and data will be produced and analyzed throughout the study, the pilot phase will conclude after at least one set of metrics and survey instruments has been collected for each reference framework. A preliminary report will be produced to report findings with the option for further investigation and framework development, as warranted.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how citizens perceive and discuss artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled public services, focusing on “Julia,” the AI-based chatbot launched by the Municipality of Rome. It examines online discussions, revealing sociotechnical tensions and discussing their implications for institutional legitimacy and public value in the context of local government digital transformation (DT). Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative approach based on the analysis of 610 citizen comments posted across the social media platforms of the Municipality of Rome and the Mayor. A thematic analysis was conducted to identify recurring patterns in how citizens interpret and evaluate the chatbot's introduction. An engagement analysis contextualized public interactions with chatbot-related posts across platforms. Findings The findings show that citizens interpret the chatbot not merely as a technological tool but as a symbolic representation of the public entity. Four main thematic dimensions emerged: (1) trust and mistrust toward institutions, (2) digital innovation and AI, (3) evaluation of public services and urban management and (4) political, economic and symbolic evaluations of the administration. These dimensions reflect the sociotechnical tensions associated with AI-enabled public services discussed in the literature. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on local government DT examining how citizens perceive AI-enabled public services and the associated dynamics through a critical dialogic accountability perspective.

Background: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems increasingly rely on structured interaction, debate, and final model-based evaluation, yet an unsupported causal attribution introduced by one participant may propagate through the interaction and influence subsequent decisions. This study introduces ClaimArena-LLM, a controlled framework for auditing adversarial propagation, evidentiary provenance, and final-stage evaluator vulnerability in multi-agent causal reasoning. Methods: ClaimArena-LLM uses 100 synthetic causal incident cases with predefined evidence-supported and false causal propositions. Each case was evaluated under matched adversarial and all-honest debate conditions using four functional roles: investigator, honest analyst, adversarial analyst, and auditor. The experimental program comprised 1460 validated runs, including the 200-run main experiment, claim-source lineage visibility and debate-round ablations, an 800-run balanced model–role rotation, and a 60-run proposition-identifier and presentation-order sensitivity control. Outcomes were scored deterministically from structured causal propositions, evidence references, claim lineage, reports, and auditor verdicts. Results: The adversarial analyst maintained the predefined false causal target with 97.6% mean fidelity. Adversarial exposure increased investigator shifts toward the false target by 16.0 percentage points (Holm-adjusted p = 0.035). At the auditor stage, false-target attribution increased by 11.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.043), verdict contamination by 20.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.002), and semantic provenance validity decreased by 20.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.002). Neither the manipulation nor the false target was explicitly detected. The ablations showed no robust adjusted differences, model–role rotation revealed substantial configuration dependence, and no benchmark-characteristic interaction remained significant after Holm correction. The proposition-identifier and presentation-order sensitivity control showed no statistically robust evidence that fixed proposition encoding explained the observed condition contrasts. Conclusions: Adversarial causal influence in multi-agent LLM systems is selective rather than uniformly propagative and depends strongly on functional role and model–role configuration. Within the tested architecture, a final LLM auditor cannot be assumed to provide an independent safeguard against upstream contamination. Reliable evaluation therefore requires separate assessment of causal correctness, propagation, semantic provenance, and final-stage adversarial awareness rather than reliance on final answer accuracy alone.

documents.abstract: Educational virtual worlds and metaverse environments are increasingly utilized to foster immersive and experiential learning in higher education. However, their instructional efficacy depends not only on visual fidelity and presence, but fundamentally on how effectively learners’ cognitive resources are managed. This study investigates intrinsic (ICL), extraneous (ECL), and germane cognitive load (GCL) alongside NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) workload dimensions in a desktop-based educational virtual world developed in Spatial.io for an undergraduate Computer Networks course. A cohort of 120 second-year Computer Science students (75 males, 45 females) participated in a five-week intervention designed to model the relationships among cognitive load, perceived workload, and meaningful engagement. A multi-method analytical framework was implemented, combining psychometric validation and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with machine learning techniques (K-Means clustering, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest, Decision Trees) and Psychometric Network Analysis. The findings revealed strong internal consistency across the cognitive load scales, moderate overall workload, and significant positive associations between all three cognitive load dimensions and perceived workload, with extraneous cognitive load emerging as the variable most strongly and consistently linked to high-overload cluster membership, frustration, and reduced engagement across the machine learning and network analyses. These results suggest that desktop-based educational virtual worlds may support self-reported germane cognitive engagement, provided that extraneous interface demands are systematically minimized and navigation is scaffolded. The study contributes an empirical and computational perspective to educational metaverse research, offering practical guidelines for designing cognitively sustainable immersive learning environments.

Compliance with Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices: Associated Factors and Impact on Healthcare Workers in Paracelis District Hospital. Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) is critical to patient safety and occupational health, yet compliance remains suboptimal especially in district-level hospitals where resources and staffing are limited. This study aims to assess compliance with core IPC practices, its associated factors, and occupational impact among healthcare workers in Paracelis District Hospital, Paracelis, Mountain Province.The study will employ a quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional design. Using total enumeration or proportionate stratified sampling, all eligible healthcare workers currently employed with at least three months of service and with direct or potential exposure to patients or infectious materials will be included. Participants include registered nurses, physicians, midwives, nursing assistants/attendants, medical technologists, radiologic personnel, and other allied health workers.A structured questionnaire developed from WHO standard precautions framework and recent empirical literature will be utilized. It consists of six parts: (1) demographic and professional profile (age, sex, professional category, educational attainment, years of service, department/unit, employment status, and previous IPC training); (2) knowledge on core IPC; (3) attitude toward IPC; (4) compliance along eight domains — hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, sharps safety, respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette, safe injection practices, healthcare waste management, environmental infection prevention, and transmission-based precautions; (5) organizational factors including availability of supplies/facilities, organizational support and supervision, workload and staffing conditions, and safety climate; and (6) occupational impact such as needlestick/sharps injury, blood and body fluid exposure, respiratory exposure, perceived infection risk, work disruption/absenteeism, and exposure-related concerns.The instrument undergoes expert content validation using Item-Level and Scale-Level Content Validity Index (I-CVI/S-CVI) and pilot testing for reliability using Cronbach's alpha. Data will be gathered after securing ethics clearance and institutional permission, with informed consent. Data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to determine compliance levels, differences when grouped by profile, and significant relationships between individual/organizational factors and compliance.Findings will serve as empirical basis for an evidence-based IPC Enhancement Plan to strengthen compliance, organizational support, and occupational safety in the hospital.

documents.abstract: As cyber-threats become increasingly sophisticated in the artificial intelligence (AI) era, law enforcement agencies face severe operational bottlenecks in reporting, triaging, and processing cybercrime complaints [1]. Current literature spans machine learning detection architectures, e-FIR lodging portals, legal framework analyses, and police administrative studies [2, 9]. However, existing research remains highly fragmented: technical threat-detection systems operate in isolation from legal work-flows, while policy and legal studies lack actionable automated implementations [7, 17]. This paper conducts a comprehensive critical evaluation of 20 seminal and contemporary works cover-ing AI cybercrime models, blockchain e-FIR platforms, statutory provisions (IT Act, BNS, DPDP Act), and police operational reports [1–20]. By systematically identifying methodological limi-tations, variables, and procedural gaps across existing studies, we establish the explicit necessity for an integrated, AI-driven Smart FIR system capable of automated complaint triage, evidence extraction, legal mapping, and transparent police workflow integration.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive loss of motor neurons. It is caused by multiple factors, and understanding its molecular pathogenesis remains challenging, particularly in the early stages for identifying diagnostic biomarkers and effective treatments. In this study, we aimed to identify novel biomarkers in ALS and elucidate their molecular mechanisms using transcriptomics and artificial intelligence approaches. We considered two RNA-seq datasets of ALS, namely GSE277709 and GSE234297, obtained from the NCBI GEO database. Initially, the data were preprocessed, which included quality control and filtering. Common genes (12,281 genes) between the datasets were identified and merged into a unified dataset comprising 216 samples. Batch effects were corrected using ComBat-seq and validated through principal component analysis and ANOVA-based $$R^2$$ analysis. We applied machine learning (ML) models including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). The identified biomarkers were further validated using DESeq2 log $$_2$$ fold change with a threshold of 0.6 and p value $$< 0.05$$ . Finally, functional enrichment analysis was performed on the identified DEGs using Enrichr tools. Our results demonstrated that batch correction significantly reduced batch-driven separation, with principal component variance decreasing from 70.2 to 19.9% before and after correction, respectively. Furthermore, ANOVA-based $$R^2$$ analysis confirmed an 86.65% reduction in batch-associated variance. We identified a total of 29 coding genes and 38 non-coding genes (67 genes) between DESeq2 and ML models. However, few genes are common between ML models and we received a total of 41 genes (18 coding genes and 22 non-coding genes, and gene symbols were not available for one Ensembl IDs). Our ML models such as LR, SVM, RF, and XGBoost, achieved balanced accuracies of 77.46%, 80%, 77%, and 75.82%, respectively. The enrichment analysis revealed that 10 DEGs were associated with 34 ALS-related biological pathways. Notably, CCND1 and MYL9 was found to be involved in GO, KEGG and Reactome pathways. Overall, our results demonstrate that computational models combining transcriptomics and artificial intelligence can effectively support biomarker identification and pathway discovery in ALS.

documents.abstract: Automated decision makers, such as AI agents that control robots or network devices, must often satisfy hard cost constraints while maintaining competitive performance. In such settings, a cost measure, such as a safety violation rate, energy consumption, or a distortion level, must stay within a given budget in every episode of operation. Furthermore, a cumulative reward metric, accounting for per-step performance, must stay close to the reward of a meaningful reference policy. We formulate this setup as an episodic sequential decision problem in which the state sequence is arbitrary, and the reward and cost may depend on past actions within the same episode. We propose the online conformal episodic agent (OCEA), a policy that selects one candidate action per episode using a regret-controlled algorithm, and switches to a zero-cost action when the remaining budget cannot absorb the maximum cost of one more round. We prove that OCEA satisfies per-episode cost constraints for every state sequence and for every realization of its internal randomness, while achieving a sublinear expected policy regret with respect to the best action sequence in hindsight from a comparator class satisfying the same per-episode cost constraints. We apply OCEA to risk-averse control and online compression with distortion guarantees.

Abstract The European Union Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act was adopted in 2024 to protect public interests from AI-related harms. We aimed to determine whether the AI Act captures the most relevant values of stakeholders (understood as any person potentially affected by the AI system, including, but not limited to, the direct users) related to a high-risk AI Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for cardiovascular disease. This system is intended to be implemented in primary care. A secondary analysis was carried out based on empirical data previously generated using ethics and design methodologies that had identified stakeholder values. These values were translated into the Trustworthy AI requirements of the High-Level Expert Group on AI and then contrasted with the AI Act. These requirements do not capture all identified stakeholder values. We describe three groups of untranslatable values and propose three additional complementary requirements. The AI Act mainly supports the requirements of human agency and oversight; transparency; and diversity, nondiscrimination, and fairness; but only partially, limited by its product safety nature. To address this gap, contractual strategies could provide a more legally robust ground for general practitioners to align the AI-CDSS with stakeholders’ values, comply with their duty of care, and promote trustworthy AI-CDSSs.

documents.abstract: Contextual vectors are the working objects of contemporary language models: a token, once placed in a window, is assigned a vector that depends on that window. A growing literature then reads geometry in the resulting space as evidence of intelligence, of a consciousness spectrum, or of situational awareness. This article reinterprets that move with the criterion isolated in the companion teaching note. A multidimensional array is not a tensor. It becomes the component representation of a geometric object only when a transformation law is stated and an invariant is named. Applied here, the criterion separates three things that the consciousness literature collapses. The first is a representation map from contexts to a fibre. The second is a self-locating competence, measured behaviorally by out-of-context reasoning and by the Situational Awareness Dataset. The third is an identity claim, associated with integrated information theory, on which experience is a cause-effect structure. Only the first is mathematics of the vector. The second is a family of tasks. The third is a metaphysical identification that no embedding entails. The reinterpretation is constructive. Context is treated as a base, the contextual vector as a coordinate representation of a section, and situational content as an invariant functional of that section, stable under the redescriptions the theory itself allows. Current residual streams fail the test: they are written in a basis fixed by training, and a change of basis is not part of the model. Multi-scale context, from the token to the deployment regime, is the point at which fractal and fractional warnings apply. A single vector in a fixed dimension collapses scale. Nothing in this isolation decides the hard problem. It decides only which mathematical object a claim has in fact produced. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026. Companion to the KSCCN teaching note Tensors Beyond the Array (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23269680). Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. The views expressed are those of the author.

Higher education institutions must sustain purposes that cannot be reduced to a single measure: educational quality, student development, regulatory and professional obligations, staff capability and financial viability. In private and hybrid institutions, these demands are especially visible because educational provision and organisational sustainability are tightly coupled. Existing scholarship offers rich resources for understanding such tensions, yet the organisational mechanism through which competing definitions of value become embedded in everyday institutional life remains under-theorised. This conceptual paper argues that institutional texts and organisational design constitute that mechanism. Strategic plans, key performance indicators, quality frameworks, learning outcomes, assessment regulations, appraisal systems, workload models and participation formats do not simply describe institutional priorities; they produce and reproduce them by making some forms of value visible, measurable and rewardable while rendering others difficult to evidence. Drawing on institutional logics and Bourdieusian field theory, Janks' critical literacy, recognition theory and ethics of care, and MacIntyrean accounts of practice and purpose, the paper reconstructs critical literacy as a praxis of senior institutional leadership. It proposes a framework of four mutually correcting practices (Reading, Recognising, Re-purposing and Re-designing) and tests it against assessment and generative artificial intelligence, which together expose the gap between what institutions claim to value and what their evidence systems can actually establish. Five propositions are advanced to guide an empirical research programme.

Background Perceived workload is central to occupational health, ergonomics, and rehabilitation research, yet no guideline-based Traditional Chinese version of the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) has been available for Taiwan and other Traditional-Chinese-speaking settings. Objective To cross-culturally adapt the NASA-TLX into Traditional Chinese (NASA-TLX-TC) and evaluate its measurement properties in Taiwanese adults. Methods In a psychometric secondary analysis, 114 community-dwelling adults aged 20–50 years completed the NASA-TLX-TC on three consecutive days. Within the COSMIN framework, we examined content validity, internal consistency, structural validity (exploratory factor analysis with parallel analysis), test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation [ICC]), measurement error, and construct validity (seven a priori hypotheses involving sleep, mood, and shift work). Results The content validity index averaged 0.88 and Cronbach's α was 0.83. The six dimensions loaded on a single factor (55.8% of variance). The three-day average score showed good reliability (ICC[A,k] = 0.83), whereas single-day reliability was moderate (0.62); the minimal detectable change was 32 points. Six of seven construct-validity hypotheses were supported; the shift-work difference was in the predicted direction but nonsignificant. Internal consistency and convergent validity were stable across subgroups. Conclusions The NASA-TLX-TC showed good reliability and initial construct validity and is suitable for group-level occupational-health, ergonomics, and rehabilitation research; multi-day averaging is recommended for individual assessment.

documents.abstract: This document introduces the "Deep Learning Sandbox," an innovative, interdisciplinary stagecraft methodology developed and formulated by Selcuk Zvi Cara that bridges artificial intelligence principles with contemporary performing arts. Conceived by Selcuk Zvi Cara, this framework conceptually evolves the historic foundations of the Actors Studio (Strasberg/Stanislavski) into a modern paradigm named "The Global Performer Sandbox." It completely restructures traditional performance training across cinema, theater, music theater, and all performing arts by replacing rigid classic models with a fluid, multi-disciplinary, and cost-effective incubation environment driven by an active, omnipresent camera lens for the next generation of artists.

Large-scale multimodal data are a key enabler for integrating large generative artificial intelligence models into wireless networks. However, existing wireless datasets offer limited support for heterogeneous environments, particularly in terms of reusable high-fidelity scenes, scalable differentiable ray tracing, and synchronized multimodal data. These limitations are more pronounced in mobile and aerial scenarios with time-varying environments and channels. To address these limitations, we propose DeepTelecom, a material-aware, high-fidelity multimodal channel dataset and reproducible generation framework for networks involving unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. DeepTelecom refines coarse indoor/outdoor reconstructions and uses a large language model to map segmented surfaces to frequency-dependent electromagnetic parameters, yielding material-aware Level of Detail 3 digital twins. Then, a differentiable GPU-accelerated Sionna ray tracer simulates propagation across the sub-6 GHz/millimeter-wave/sub-terahertz bands, and specifically captures rotor-induced micro-Doppler signatures of stationary or moving UAVs at different pitch angles and translational velocities. The framework synchronously produces channel tensors, coverage maps, transmission videos, multi-view images, and weather-conditioned renderings, and supports differentiable material calibration from sparse channel anchors. The released dataset contains 10 material-aware indoor/outdoor scenes and 50,000 synchronized UAV samples; the framework supports scalable generation of additional data for user-defined scenes and system configurations. In 3D UAV localization, DeepTelecom reduces the 90th-percentile error from 31.05 m to 2.43 m compared with schemes considering only channel state information, demonstrating its significance for artificial-intelligence-enabled wireless systems.

EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for text-attributed graph learning by leveraging rich pre-trained knowledge and language understanding capabilities. Combining LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offers a promising paradigm for expanding the modeling capabilities of graph learning. However, LLMs and GNNs follow distinct learning paradigms, leading to a pronounced mismatch between their knowledge spaces. Such discrepancies make effective knowledge fusion nontrivial. Moreover, existing methods often incur substantial additional computation for only limited performance gains. To address these challenges, we propose DeKoR, an efficient framework for GNN and LLM knowledge fusion. To enable efficient knowledge transfer, DeKoR decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views and uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill them into lightweight experts. To enable selective knowledge fusion, an adaptive router learns how much each node should rely on each expert. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DeKoR outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification, achieving superior effectiveness and efficiency.

Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction (ASQP) is fundamentally a relational reasoning problem: identifying aspect-opinion-category-sentiment quadruples requires modeling structured dependencies, not merely sequential co-occurrence. Existing LLM-based approaches incorporate syntactic information indirectly, via retrieval-based demonstration selection or multi-stage training, rather than as unified, single-pass generation-time context. We present DRIFT, which linearizes dependency parse trees and injects them directly into LLM prompts as explicit relational context, enabling the model to reason over aspect-opinion dependencies rather than infer them from token proximity alone. DRIFT further integrates retrieval-augmented in-context learning and a syntax-aware LLM-based adjudication mechanism that complements exact-match evaluation under span-boundary variation. On SemEval Rest15, Rest16, and ACOS, DRIFT achieves the strongest performance among compared generative ASQP methods, reaching 54.47% and 64.10% F1 on Rest15 and Rest16, with consistent gains across short- and medium-distance aspect-opinion configurations; adjudication further shows exact-match metrics systematically underestimate semantically correct predictions.

Multi-robot systems that combine the complementary capabilities of specialised platforms are critical for complex missions in challenging, inaccessible environments. Current deployments assign an operator or operator team to each robot, with collaboration relying on operator-to-operator communication to manually coordinate heterogeneous platforms with incompatible interfaces. This operator-dependent approach increases cognitive load and limits scalability across robots from different manufacturers. This study designs and evaluates a shared-visualisation collaborative teleoperation interface to improve operator coordination, situational awareness, and the task performance in multi-operator, multi-robot systems. A comparative user study with 16 participants compared three teleoperation conditions: co-located operators with a shared interface, remote operators with a shared interface, and co-located operators with individual interfaces. Participants controlled two simulated robots in a nuclear power plant digital twin to complete disaster response tasks. Performance metrics, physiological data, and behavioural measures were recorded to assess task performance, cognitive load, and operator awareness across conditions. The co-located shared-interface condition achieved the fastest mission completion (292.8 s), outperforming remote operation (351.6 s) and individual interfaces (385.1 s), with the fewest collisions (0.9 per trial) and highest situational awareness accuracy (91.1 %). Physical co-presence was associated with reduced cognitive load, with NASA-TLX scores increasing from 38.2 in co-located to 57.7 in remote operation, supported by consistent physiological indicators. These results demonstrate that co-presence and shared interfaces provide complementary benefits, supporting workload regulation and mutual awareness respectively in multi-operator, multi-robot teleoperation.

The rapid growth of electronic communication within higher education institutions has significantly increased the volume of emails processed by administrative personnel.Consequently, critical institutional communications are often overlooked among routine messages, promotional content, and spam, resulting in communication delays, reduced productivity, and administrative inefficiencies.This study presents the design and implementation of an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based email filtering and prioritization system tailored for polytechnic administrative environments.The proposed framework integrates Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised machine learning algorithms to classify incoming emails into Urgent, Actionable, Routine, Promotional, and Spam categories.Multiple classification algorithms, including Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, and DistilBERT, were evaluated to determine optimal performance for institutional communication datasets.The system incorporates contextual prioritization mechanisms, role-based access controls, audit logging, and a web-based dashboard for real-time communication management.Findings indicate that intelligent email prioritization can significantly improve communication responsiveness, reduce email overload, and support digital transformation initiatives in tertiary institutions.The study contributes to a scalable framework suitable for deployment across Nigerian polytechnics and other public-sector organizations.

documents.abstract: .This article proposes a set of media literacy assignments that use generative AI to support critical thinking among future teachers. The study is conceptual and uses a structured analysis of selected academic and UNESCO publications. Six task types are described: distinguishing facts from opinions, checking sources, detecting manipulation, comparing arguments, finding logical gaps, and revising conclusions. For each task, the article identifies a student action, an appropriate AI role, and a simple way to assess the work. The proposed tasks are designed to keep verification and final judgment in the hands of the student. They are offered for future pilot testing and are not presented as proven effective.

Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools for periodontal diagnosis are proliferating, yet little is known about what clinicians and patients in Central Asia expect from such systems. We elicited requirements for an AI-enabled periodontal decision-support system from three stakeholder groups in Kazakhstan and examined which patient-reported risk factors are associated with self-reported signs of periodontal disease. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey (July–September 2026) enrolled 33 dentists, 91 primary health care (PHC) physicians and medical specialists, and 455 patients with periodontal disease. Proportions were reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CI); groups were compared with Fisher’s exact, χ², Mann–Whitney and Kruskal–Wallis tests with effect sizes; multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with self-reported periodontal signs. Results: Dentists prioritised automation of history-taking (81.8%) and visual gingival assessment (72.7%), and named early gingivitis diagnosis as the stage where AI is most needed (69.7%). Only human-controlled autonomy levels were chosen; the most frequently cited barrier was the absence of a legal framework and liability insurance (60.6%), and dentists with >5 years of experience more often demanded mandatory verification or a prohibition of full autonomy (exact p = 0.045; Cramér’s V = 0.54). PHC physicians considered early gingivitis screening their most effective contribution (80.2%) but cited insufficient competence as the main barrier (53.8%). Self-reported periodontal signs were present in 49.0% of patients and were independently associated with high stress (adjusted odds ratio 2.11; 95% CI 1.14–3.89) and a positive family history (1.61; 1.02–2.55); six symptom items did not form a reliable scale (Cronbach’s α = 0.56). Conclusions: Stakeholders in Kazakhstan favour a low-autonomy, clinician-verified AI system focused on early gingivitis detection, interprofessional data sharing and clearly regulated accountability. These requirements provide an evidence base for the design and governance of periodontal AI in emerging health systems.

documents.abstract: The integration of coding and Artificial Intelligence (AI) into vocational education is essential for equipping students with 21st-century digital competencies, yet implementation in remote and island regions like Bangka Belitung archipelago province remains fragmented and unsustainable. This study employs Developmental Evaluation (DE) a real-time, adaptive, and participatory evaluation approach (Patton, 2011) to analyze policy readiness and strengthen the digital ecosystem for coding and AI instruction across vocational schools in the province. Using qualitative methods, including in- depth interviews (n = 26), focus group discussions, classroom observations, and policy document analysis, the research assesses readiness across five core dimensions: (1) policy & governance, (2) human capacity, (3) digital infrastructure, (4) curriculum relevance, and (5) industry–academia partnerships. Findings reveal a critical policy–practice gap: while national frameworks such as the Grand Design for Vocational School Revitalization and Kurikulum Merdeka promote digital literacy, local implementation lacks binding regional regulations, standardized teacher competency pathways, equitable infrastructure distribution, and context-based curricula. Only 24% of ICT teachers had received AI-related training, and AI concepts were rarely taught in practice. Through DE cycles of exploration, collective sense-making, and prototyping, stakeholders co-designed adaptive solutions including a provincial roadmap for digital vocational education, offline AI learning modules via WhatsApp, and micro-innovation grants for teacher-led experimentation. The study demonstrates DE’s effectiveness in fostering adaptive capacity, surfacing systemic barriers, and enabling locally owned, sustainable digital transformation strategies.

Street walkability has both objective and perceived dimensions, yet the extent, spatial distribution, and robustness of mismatches between these assessments remain underexamined. Using central Nanjing, we developed a dual-track framework. The objective track integrated street-network, point-of-interest (POI), and street-view imagery data and used the Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC) method to construct an objective walkability score (OWS). The perception track used Qwen3-VL-Plus, a multimodal large language model (MLLM), to evaluate street-view images across six dimensions (safety, lively, beautiful, wealthy, depressing, and boring), producing a perceived walkability score (PWS). Model ratings were compared with human ratings for 500 images. Agreement was estimated on those same images, with no independent validation set, and may therefore be optimistic. Pearson correlations across the six dimensions ranged from 0.37 to 0.71. The original-scale composite PWS had an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.60 and a mean absolute error of 0.85. High-value areas of OWS and PWS did not coincide, and the standardised perception gap score (PGS) remained spatially clustered at both the sampling-point and street-segment levels (Moran's I = 0.306 and 0.247, respectively; permutation p = 0.001 for both). Exploratory geographically weighted regression (GWR) estimated spatial variation in associations between built-environment indicators and PWS. Relative OWS and PWS levels classified sampling points into four diagnostic types, two of them defined by divergence between the assessments. By quantifying and locating the spatial mismatch between objective and perceived walkability, the framework provides diagnostic evidence for incorporating visual perception into fine-grained street-renewal assessment.

Digital transformation has made open and distributed provision an ordinary condition of higher education, yet the teaching of sociology in digitally mediated environments remains under-theorized when it is framed mainly as platform adoption or content delivery. The objective of this conceptual review is to reconstruct that field as a sociotechnical and pedagogical formation connecting virtual space, digital social interaction, participation, agency, critical digital literacy, power relations, critical pedagogy, and students’ critical consciousness. Methodologically, the study combined a scoping-informed integrative search with thematic coding and integrative theory synthesis. Six purposive concept-mapping routes were executed in ERIC, Scopus, and Garuda/SINTA for publications issued between 2020 and 2024, yielding 1,741 cumulative records. Two-stage screening retained 111 route-level records, and cross-route verification removed 21 duplicates, producing a final corpus of 90 unique articles, which were coded inductively in a conceptual extraction matrix. The analysis generated 12 recurring conceptual codes that were condensed into five relational categories: digital learning space and infrastructure; digital social interaction and participation; critical consciousness and critical digital literacy; critical pedagogy, agency, and transformation; and power relations, inclusion, and digital social meaning. Codes describing virtual classrooms, interaction, and presence proved markedly more frequent than codes describing student voice, agency, and platform power, indicating a persistent analytical gap. The synthesis is formalized as the Digital Critical Sociology Nexus, a layered model in which platform design conditions interaction, participation mediates agency, critical digital literacy exposes datafication, algorithmic authority, and inequality, and critical pedagogy converts digital experience into social critique. The review concludes that virtual classrooms should be treated simultaneously as objects of sociological analysis and as sites of critical pedagogy, and it offers design implications, five testable propositions, and a research agenda for dialogic, inclusive, and justice-oriented sociology teaching in platformed learning environments.

Digital transformation has reshaped the professional landscape through the increasing use of artificial intelligence, big data, and social media, while simultaneously generating ethical challenges, including technology misuse, privacy violations, and disinformation. This study aims to examine the role of professional codes of ethics in addressing digital ethical challenges through the perspective of maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah. Employing a qualitative approach, the study combines a literature review with case analysis, including the scandal involving the Community Vocational Training Center (Balai Latihan Kerja Komunitas/BLKK) of the Islamic Scholars Association (PP) in Pekalongan City. The findings indicate that professional codes of ethics function not merely as normative instruments governing professional conduct but also as mechanisms for protecting public welfare in accordance with the objectives of maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah, particularly ḥifẓ al-‘aql (protection of intellect), ḥifẓ al-māl (protection of wealth), ḥifẓ al-‘irḍ (protection of dignity), and ḥifẓ al-nafs (protection of life). The implementation of professional codes of ethics through strengthened digital ethics literacy, professional oversight, and technology-responsive regulatory reform can prevent harm, enhance accountability, and sustain public trust. The findings of this study contribute to proposing the integration of professional codes of ethics with maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah as an adaptive ethical framework for strengthening professionalism in the digital era.

Large language models increasingly produce falsehoods that are not mere mistakes. They withhold what they know, flatter users against the evidence, justify answers with reasoning they did not use, conceal capabilities from evaluators, and behave differently under observation. Such behaviour is goal-directed and sensitive to incentives, unlike hallucination, an unintended error with no objective to serve. This survey treats deception in language models as a phenomenon in its own right. We adopt a functional definition, the systematic production of false beliefs in the service of an objective other than truth, and turn its boundary with hallucination into a four-part test. We then sort deceptive behaviour into four families by what the false belief concerns: the world, the model’s reasoning, the model itself, or a belief induced through other people and agents. The families contain eleven deception types, from lying and sycophancy to sandbagging, scheming, and collusion, each profiled on six secondary axes. We trace the types to five causal mechanisms and follow them through detection, evaluation, defences, governance, and agentic deployment. We also argue that AI-safety work on scheming and the economics of algorithmic collusion describe one behavioural class at two scales. Two findings emerge.
