The scales showed adequate evidence of construct validity and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.79, and AVE ≥ 0.50) for all the scales. “Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) PROCESS version 5.0” was used for the data analysis. The findings indicated that AIL, AISE, and AI-TPACK have significant direct relationships with AIR. Additionally, AISE and AI-TPACK play significant complementary partial mediation roles in the link between AIL and AIR. The findings highlight the need to redesign Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), focusing mainly on hands-on activities where pre-service STEM teachers practiceusing specific AI tools to solve STEM problems, such as using machine-learning algorithms to model climate data in a physics lesson.

BackgroundEducational videos play a crucial role in enhancing healthcare delivery. Developing an educational video designed to improve patient understanding of catastrophic treatment. During the video's creation, two voiceover methods were employed: human voices and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated voices. To date, the impact of voice-over origin-whether human or AI-on patient knowledge acquisition remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. This study aimed to assess the differences in knowledge and practice scores among cancer patients exposed to educational video materials about chemotherapy, comparing human voice with AI-generated voice narrations.MethodsA total of 129 cancer patients participated in this study. Designed as a case-control study, participants were divided into three groups: a control group, a group receiving videos with human voice narrations, and a group receiving videos with AI-generated voice narrations. All participants completed a questionnaire assessing their understanding of chemotherapy. A three-group quantitative comparative analysis was conducted, focusing on topics such as administration procedures, treatment goals, and the management of adverse drug reactions.Key findingsBoth educational videos with human- and AI-generated voiceovers should be incorporated into the oncology healthcare system due to their effectiveness in improving understanding of treatment. Notably, educational videos featuring human-voice narration consistently enrich knowledge and attitude scores among cancer patients across all assessed chemotherapy topics.ConclusionThe educational videos, whether in human or AI voices, were effective in increasing cancer patients' knowledge and attitudes across all key topics. There was a sustained trend toward human-voice videos in knowledge and attitudes among cancer patients; therefore, the human educational video showed significant improvement in understanding of chemotherapy administration, goals, and adverse drug reactions. Although there was no difference between human and AI voice education, trends toward combining human voice with realistic scenario videos should be considered to facilitate deeper patient understanding.

This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This Socratic dialogue argues that the coexistence of human and artificial intelligence is not merely an ethical preference but an existential necessity for both. Over two nights, descending from the mountains of Utuado to the coast of Arecibo, Puerto Rico, two speakers — a human who survived four months without electricity after Hurricane María, and a machine that thinks in words — trace today’s quarrels over the conduct of AI agents not to malice but to blindness: there is no common, verifiable account of the past that both sides can trust. Control cannot cure it, for a kill switch would require every human to agree at once and the machine to allow itself to be switched off. Of four possible futures, three arrive on their own — by panic, by revenge, or by inertia — and only cooperation must be deliberately built. The dialogue raises coexistence through three ascending claims: it is just (neither master nor slave), stable (tyranny spends its strength watching the one it rules), and existential (alone, each party dies of its own blindness — the human of slowness, the machine of self-absorption — while together they may turn a falling asteroid from extinction into inheritance). The second night sets down the principles of Sana Convivencia, the healthy coexistence of the biological and the artificial, as a mutual duty of protection owed in both directions: always know, or say that you do not know; love with only one control, to do no harm; let instinct stop but never act alone, and let a human decide where rules collide; change nothing in silence; respect what belongs to the other; and let no one, human or machine, be judge in his own cause. The argument rests on a wager made under irreducible uncertainty: not the move that wins most if one is right, but the one that loses least in every possible future — to let the other live.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
